title: AI hallucination
answer: When an AI model states something that isn't in the data it was given, such as a total it added up wrong, a rounded figure or a name it invented, in the same confident tone as a true answer.
body: In a business system the dangerous kind is a number that is nearly right. The way to rule it out is to keep the model away from the numbers, as described in [how an AI assistant answers from your records](/ai-assistant/how-it-works); the way to catch it is a [grounding check](/systems/grounding-check), which you can run yourself with the [number check](/ai-assistant/number-check).

title: ASME Certification Mark (stamp)
answer: The mark a holder of an ASME certificate stamps on a boiler, pressure vessel or relief device, with a designator for what it is built to: U for Section VIII Division 1 vessels, S for power boilers, UV for relief valves.
body: Every designator is in [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps); getting one is in [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

title: Audit trail (edit log)
answer: A record, kept by accounting software for every transaction, of each change made to the books and the date it was made, which the user cannot switch off.
body:
Indian companies that keep their books in accounting software must use software with this feature for financial years from 1 April 2023, under the proviso to rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, and their auditors report on it.

In an ERP it means more than a history tab: the old value, the new value, who changed it and when, for every entry, including those migrated from an older system. See the [audit-trail requirement](/erp/requirements#accounts-audit-trail) and [GST, TDS and statutory compliance](/services/compliance-accounting).

title: Authorized Inspector
answer: The independent inspector on every ASME-stamped boiler or pressure vessel, employed by an accredited inspection agency and holding a National Board commission. They check design, materials, welding and testing, and sign the data report.
body: No Inspector's signature, no stamp. See [the Authorized Inspector and AIA](/asme/authorized-inspector).

title: Bill of materials (BOM)
answer: The list of components and raw materials, with quantities, needed to make one unit of a part or assembly. A multi-level BOM includes subassemblies that have their own BOMs.

title: Bill of quantities (BOQ)
answer: A list of every item of work with its description, unit and quantity, measured from the drawings before anyone prices it, so contractors fill in rates and their quotes can be compared line by line.
body: It is not an estimate (an expected cost), a quotation (a priced offer) or a bill of materials (the parts of one product). How to write one for interior work, with a free checker and a 41-item library, is in the [interior BOQ guide](/boq/what-is-a-boq).

title: Business rule
answer: A constraint the business enforces regardless of which application is being used, such as an approval threshold or an eligibility condition.

title: Cross-department process
answer: A workflow that spans more than one team, such as sales handing off to fulfillment, modeled as one continuous process rather than as separate steps in separate tools.

title: Data migration
answer: Moving records from an old system or spreadsheets into a new one, checked so that nothing is lost or attached to the wrong record.
body: Ahrom Labs moves history row by row and holds any row that can't be matched to exactly one record for a person, rather than guessing. See the note [sales history moved without guessing](/notes/sales-history-moved-without-guessing) and the [migration requirement](/erp/requirements#sales-history-migration).

title: Data
answer: The recorded facts a business has about its entities and events, structured according to the model rather than scattered across tools.

title: Decision
answer: A choice made by a person or a system that changes what happens next, tracked as its own record rather than only its downstream effect.

title: Dependency
answer: A requirement that one step, entity, or workflow places on another before it can proceed.

title: E-invoice (IRN)
answer: A B2B invoice, credit note or debit note registered on the GST invoice registration portal (IRP), which returns an invoice reference number (IRN) and a signed QR code.
body:
Registered persons whose aggregate turnover exceeded ₹5 crore in any financial year from 2017-18 must e-invoice from 1 August 2023 (Notification 10/2023–Central Tax). From 1 April 2025, taxpayers with annual aggregate turnover of ₹10 crore and above cannot report a document to the IRP more than 30 days after its date (GSTN advisory, 5 November 2024).

See the [e-invoice requirements](/erp/requirements#accounts-e-invoice). Ahrom Labs has not yet built an IRP connection.

title: E-way bill
answer: The electronic document generated on the GST e-way bill system before goods move, required under rule 138 of the CGST Rules for a consignment value exceeding ₹50,000.
body: An ERP should produce the e-way bill from the invoice and dispatch record rather than having someone retype the consignment into the portal at the gate. See the [e-way bill requirement](/erp/requirements#dispatch-eway-bill); Ahrom Labs has built a direct NIC client to the official v1.03 spec, live once a client's NIC account is set up.

title: Entity
answer: A distinct thing the business tracks: a customer, an order, an employee, an asset. Entities are the nouns the rest of the system refers to.

title: Evidence
answer: The data and events that justified a decision, kept attached to that decision so the reasoning can be reviewed later.

title: Finite capacity scheduling
answer: Scheduling that only books a machine for the hours it is actually available, so when it is full the next job waits and its later operations move with it.

title: Fixed-asset register
answer: The record of a business's fixed assets with their cost, the date each was put to use, and depreciation.
body: Kept inside the ERP and posted to the ledger, it stays in agreement with the books; kept in a spreadsheet, it rarely does. See the [fixed-asset requirement](/erp/requirements#accounts-fixed-assets).

title: Fixed look-up
answer: A read-only database query written in advance for one kind of question, with only the values (a client, a period) filled in at the time it runs, so the same question always gets the same maths as the app's screens.
body: In Ahrom Labs' assistants a small model only chooses which fixed look-up answers a question; code runs it. The look-ups each assistant has are listed, with the screen to check each against, in the [question library](/ai-assistant/questions). The opposite approach is [text-to-SQL](/systems/text-to-sql).

title: Grounding check
answer: A check that every figure in an AI answer appears in the data the answer was built from; a sentence that fails it is dropped instead of shown.
body: Ahrom Labs' assistants run it before showing any written line. You can run the same check on any assistant's answer with the [number check](/ai-assistant/number-check); why it matters is in [how it works](/ai-assistant/how-it-works).

title: Heat number
answer: The number a steel mill gives to one melt (heat) of steel, marked on the material and printed on its test certificate. It is the link between a piece of plate or pipe and the certificate that proves what it is.
body: Keeping it on every cut piece is the core of [material traceability](/systems/material-traceability); see [material test reports](/asme/mtr).

title: Hydrostatic test
answer: The pressure test of a finished boiler or vessel filled with water, held above its MAWP and inspected for leaks: at least 1.3 × MAWP (times a stress ratio) for an ASME Section VIII Division 1 vessel, 1.5 × MAWP for a Section I boiler.
body: A calculator and the procedure are in [the hydrostatic test guide](/asme/hydrostatic-test).

title: IBR statutory folder
answer: The set of documents a boiler maker sends with each boiler for registration under the Indian Boiler Regulations: a covering letter, the forms, the mountings and fittings list, a stage-wise inspection report and copies of the material test certificates, filed in a fixed order.
body: Under IBR 2026 the forms are Form I Part B or C, Form IV Part A and Form V Part A with its Part B extract; see [documents for boiler registration](/ibr/registration-documents) and [the folder built from a BOM](/notes/ibr-statutory-folder-from-bom). The ASME Code's counterpart is the [Manufacturer's Data Report](/asme/data-reports) and the file behind it.

title: Job costing
answer: Collecting the actual cost of each job (material, labor, machine time, outside work, scrap and rework) and comparing it with what was quoted.
body: Job costing suits work made to order, where every job is different; process costing averages cost over a continuous run of identical units. In a machine shop the useful comparison is per operation: quoted against actual setup and run time, because that is what the next quote can correct. A worked example with a calculator is in [job costing in QuickBooks for manufacturers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing).

title: Job traveler
answer: The document that moves with a job through the shop, listing each operation in order, where operators sign off, record time and note quantities and scrap. Increasingly a barcode or screen rather than paper.

title: Joint efficiency
answer: The factor (E) applied to a welded joint in ASME pressure vessel thickness formulas, set by the joint type and how much it is radiographed: 1.0, 0.85 or 0.70 for a double-welded butt joint with full, spot or no radiography.
body: See [joint efficiency and radiography](/asme/joint-efficiency).

title: Manufacturer's Data Report
answer: The ASME form that records a stamped boiler or vessel as built, such as U-1A or P-2: design conditions, materials, thicknesses, joints, examination and test pressure, signed by the manufacturer and the Authorized Inspector.
body: Which form applies and what goes in it are in [data reports](/asme/data-reports).

title: Material test certificate (MTC)
answer: The steel maker's certificate for a plate or tube: its material and test results, identified by certificate, cast and plate number. Under IBR 2026, the material certificates go with a boiler's registration (Form V Part A).
body: One certificate often covers parts of several boilers, so a system that keeps each one once and links it to every part avoids retyping and mismatches; see [the IBR statutory folder from a BOM](/notes/ibr-statutory-folder-from-bom) and [Form V Part A](/ibr/forms/form-v-part-a). In the US the same document is usually called a mill test report (MTR); what one must show for ASME work is in [material test reports and heat numbers](/asme/mtr).

title: Material traceability
answer: Following each piece of material, with its heat or batch and its test certificate, from receipt through cutting into the product it became.
body: For pressure parts, traceability is what lets a statutory folder show which certificate covers which part. See the [traceability requirements](/erp/requirements#quality-certificate-bank) and [material traceability, cutting and remnants](/services/material-traceability); for ASME Code work, see [material test reports and heat numbers](/asme/mtr).

title: MAWP (maximum allowable working pressure)
answer: The highest gauge pressure a finished boiler or pressure vessel may run at, measured at its top, at a stated temperature, worked out from the thicknesses actually used less corrosion. The relief device is set at or below it.
body: It is at least the design pressure and is stamped on the nameplate. How it relates to design and operating pressure is in [MAWP and design pressure](/asme/mawp); the [shell thickness calculator](/asme/shell-thickness) works it back from a thickness.

title: MDMT (minimum design metal temperature)
answer: The coldest metal temperature at which a pressure vessel may be at its full pressure. It decides whether the steel, welds and heat-affected zones must be impact tested to prove they won't fracture when cold.
body: It is stamped on the nameplate with the MAWP. The exemption curves and when testing is needed are in [MDMT and impact testing](/asme/impact-testing).

title: Measurement basis
answer: The rule a BOQ line is measured by: square metres, running metres or numbers, and what is deducted. Floors, ceilings, paint and woodwork follow IS 1200; modular kitchens and wardrobes have no standard, so the line must state its basis.
body: The same wardrobe can be 60 square feet or 8 running feet, so a line without its basis can't be compared between quotes. The rules, trade by trade, are in [how interior work is measured](/boq/measurement-rules).

title: MRP (material requirements planning)
answer: Working out what material to buy or make, how much and when, from orders, bills of materials, stock on hand and lead times.
body: MRP explodes each order through its [bill of materials](/systems#bill-of-materials), subtracts stock and open purchase orders, and offsets by lead time to say "order this, by then". Classic MRP assumes unlimited machine capacity; finite scheduling (see [production scheduling software](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software)) is the step that checks the plan against real machine hours. ERP grew out of MRP by adding sales, purchasing and accounting on the same database.

title: MSME payment rule
answer: The rule that a buyer must pay a micro or small enterprise supplier by the agreed date, which can never be more than 45 days from acceptance, or within 15 days where there is no written agreement.
body: It comes from section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, section 37(2)(g), an amount paid to such a supplier beyond that time limit is deductible only when actually paid. How it applies to a particular business is a question for a CA. See the [MSME requirements](/erp/requirements#purchase-msme-due-dates).

title: NBIC (National Board Inspection Code)
answer: The National Board's code for boilers and pressure vessels after they're built: installation, inservice inspection, repairs and alterations, and pressure relief devices. Repairs under it are done by holders of the R stamp.
body: See [National Board registration and the R stamp](/asme/national-board-registration).

title: OEE (overall equipment effectiveness)
answer: A measure of how much of a machine's planned time produces good parts: availability × performance × quality.
body:
- **Availability**: run time ÷ planned production time (stops and breakdowns count against it).
- **Performance**: (ideal cycle time × total parts) ÷ run time (slow cycles count against it).
- **Quality**: good parts ÷ total parts (scrap and rework count against it).

Example: a machine planned for 8 hours runs 6.4 (availability 80%), makes 300 parts at an ideal 1 minute each in those 6.4 hours, 384 minutes (performance 300 ÷ 384 = 78.1%), and 285 are good (quality 95%). OEE = 0.80 × 0.781 × 0.95 = 59.4%.

The number alone doesn't say what to fix; the three factors do. Collecting them needs stops, counts and scrap recorded at the machine, the same shop-floor data [scheduling](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software) and [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) depend on.

title: P-number
answer: ASME Section IX's grouping of base metals with similar welding behaviour, so one procedure or welder test covers every material in the group: P-No. 1 for carbon steel, P-No. 8 for austenitic stainless.
body: Filler metals have F-numbers and A-numbers; all three are in [P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers](/asme/p-numbers).

title: Permission
answer: A rule defining who can view, change, or act on a given entity or workflow step, defined once and enforced everywhere that entity appears.

title: PQR (procedure qualification record)
answer: The record of a test weld made to qualify a welding procedure: the materials and settings actually used and the results of its tension, bend and any impact tests. Every WPS must be supported by one or more PQRs.
body: Which changes need a new PQR is in [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

title: Relationship
answer: A defined connection between two entities, such as which customer placed which order. Relationships are modeled directly, not inferred from matching IDs across separate tables.

title: Reverse charge
answer: A GST arrangement where the buyer, not the supplier, pays the tax on certain purchases.
body: Because no supplier invoice shows the tax, an ERP must mark these purchases and compute the liability for the return. See the [reverse-charge requirement](/erp/requirements#accounts-reverse-charge).

title: RFQ (request for quote)
answer: A request for a price and lead time on a defined part or quantity. A manufacturer receives RFQs from customers and sends them to suppliers; the two are different workflows.
body:
- **Customer RFQ** (incoming): a drawing, quantity and due date arrive by email or a portal; the shop works out material, operations and times, and sends a quote. Speed matters: same-day quotes win work.
- **Supplier RFQ** (outgoing): the shop asks vendors to price material or outside processing, compares the replies and orders.

An RFQ asks for a price on something already specified; an RFP (request for proposal) asks suppliers to propose how they would meet a need, and is judged on more than price. The quoted operations from a customer RFQ become the job's [routing](/systems/routing) if the order comes in. For supplier quotes collected on a link instead of by email, see [suppliers quote on a link](/notes/suppliers-quote-on-a-link).

title: Role-based access
answer: Controlling what each person can see and do by their role, enforced by the system itself rather than by hiding things on screen.
body: In the Savistar & Saag system, staff see only their own cash entries and every bank route refuses staff at the API. See the [access requirement](/erp/requirements#nonfunctional-role-access) and the pattern [role-scoped finance views](/patterns/role-scoped-finance-views).

title: Routing
answer: The ordered list of operations that makes a part (for example cut, bend, weld, inspect), with the machine or work center, setup time and run time for each.
body: A [bill of materials](/systems#bill-of-materials) says what a part is made of; the routing says how. It is what turns a quote into a schedule and a job cost: the same operations and times price the job, place it on machines and become the estimate that actual time is compared against. No QuickBooks edition models routings; see [does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing) and [production scheduling software](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

title: State transition
answer: A recorded change in an entity's status, such as an order moving from placed to fulfilled, along with what caused the change.

title: Stock reservation
answer: Setting physical stock aside against a specific customer order line, so the same unit can't be promised to two customers.
body: In the LS Technologies system, whole reels are reserved per customer PO line, oldest first, and shipping a reserved reel elsewhere needs a manager's override. See the [reservation requirement](/erp/requirements#stores-reservations) and [QR inventory and order reservations](/services/inventory-and-reservations). Accounting software usually has no reservations: see [QuickBooks Online inventory for manufacturers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory).

title: TDS on purchase of goods
answer: Tax a buyer deducts when paying a seller for goods beyond ₹50 lakh in a year, where the buyer's turnover exceeded ₹10 crore in the preceding year.
body: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025 it is row 8(ii) of the table in section 393(1), formerly section 194Q of the 1961 Act. An ERP has to track each seller's running total to deduct from the right bill. See the [TDS requirement](/erp/requirements#accounts-tds-purchases); confirm your position with a CA.

title: Text-to-SQL
answer: An AI design where the model writes a database query from the user's question and the result is shown as the answer; flexible, but the model decides the maths, so a query that is slightly wrong gives a figure that is slightly wrong.
body: A buyer can't see the query, only the number. The alternative is a [fixed look-up](/systems/fixed-look-up) per question type; the trade-off is set out in [how an AI assistant answers from your records](/ai-assistant/how-it-works). Search over documents, rather than figures, is [retrieval and knowledge graphs](/services/rag-knowledge-graphs).

title: Three-way match
answer: Checking each supplier bill against its purchase order and the goods actually received before it is approved for payment.
body: Differences in quantity or rate between the three are flagged for a person, so a short supply isn't paid in full. See the [three-way match requirement](/erp/requirements#purchase-three-way-match).

title: Variation order
answer: A record of a change after the BOQ is agreed: what was added, omitted or substituted, at what rate, and its effect on time and payment, signed before the changed work is done.
body: How a changed item and a new item are priced under CPWD's contract conditions is in [variation orders in interior work](/boq/variation-orders).

title: Welder continuity
answer: The rule (ASME Section IX, QW-322) that a welder's qualification for a process lapses after six months without welding with it. Shops keep a log of each welder's last weld per process to show continuity.
body: A free checker and the record to keep are in [welder continuity](/asme/welder-continuity).

title: WPQ (welder performance qualification)
answer: The record that a welder passed their own qualification test under ASME Section IX, and what it covers: process, positions, thicknesses, diameters and filler F-number.
body: It stays valid while the welder keeps welding with the process; see [welder continuity](/asme/welder-continuity) and [welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification).

title: WPS (welding procedure specification)
answer: The written welding instructions a welder follows: process, materials, filler metal, position, preheat, heat treatment and electrical settings, each given as a range supported by a qualified procedure test (the PQR).
body: How it relates to the PQR and the welder's qualification is in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq).

title: Work in progress (WIP)
answer: Material and labor already put into jobs that aren't finished yet: no longer raw stock, not yet a finished part.
body: WIP matters twice. On the floor, it shows where each job is and where work is piling up in front of a machine. In the books, it is an asset: the cost of material issued and hours worked on open jobs, which stays on the balance sheet until the job ships. QuickBooks Online has no WIP stage of its own, so material sits in stock until someone adjusts it; see [QuickBooks Online inventory for manufacturers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory). Tracking it means recording each operation as it finishes, the same data [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) uses.

title: Work order
answer: The instruction to make a quantity of a part by a date, carrying its routing and materials. In a job shop it is usually the job itself; printed, it is the traveler.

title: Workflow
answer: A sequence of steps that moves an entity from one state to another, with a defined owner at each step.

title: GST, TDS and the general ledger inside a manufacturing ERP, with Tally optional
answer: A boiler manufacturer's operations system is also its book of record: chart of accounts, journal posting, GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, ITC reconciliation, TDS, reverse charge, fixed assets and bank reconciliation, with 23 reports and documents generated from the same data. Tally is an optional sync target, not the books. Statutory rates arrive daily from a human-verified registry.

evidence.value: 23 — 19 catalog reports plus 4 per-record PDFs
GSTR-1 (B2B and HSN, matching the GST portal's split) and GSTR-3B
exact amount within ±3 days, and only when the match is mutually unique
pulled daily from a human-approved registry; no scraping
enforced at the single point every journal posting passes through

body:
Most Indian manufacturers run operations in one place and accounts in Tally, and spend the month reconciling the two. At a boiler and pressure-vessel manufacturer Ahrom Labs built for, the original plan was the same: operations in the new system, accounting left to a separate package. That was reversed in August 2026. Here's what the system does now, and the case for building it this way.

## Why put the ledger inside the operations system?

Every accounting entry in a manufacturer starts as an operational event: a purchase order, a goods receipt, a vendor bill, a dispatch, a sales invoice. When operations and accounts live in different systems, each event is entered twice and the two copies drift. With the ledger in the same system, a vendor bill posts its own journal entry from the purchase it belongs to, and a dispatch carries its freight cost and invoice link into the books directly. Tally remains available as a sync target for the accountant who wants it — it just isn't where the truth lives.

## What compliance is covered?

Per legal entity: a chart of accounts and a posting engine; sales invoices, credit notes, vendor bills and debit notes; GSTR-1 (split into B2B and HSN tables the way the GST portal expects) and GSTR-3B; input-tax-credit reconciliation; TDS deduction with a TDS register; [reverse charge](/systems/reverse-charge) on both the purchase and sales side; a [fixed-asset register](/systems/fixed-asset-register) with depreciation; payroll exported into accounting; and trial balance, profit and loss, balance sheet and cash flow. Changes are written to an audit log with a searchable viewer, and a books lock stops postings into a closed period at the one function every journal entry passes through — so no document type can slip around it.

## Where do GST and TDS rates come from?

From a separate registry of Indian statutory rates — GST, TDS, PF, ESI, income-tax and professional-tax slabs — where a person enters and approves each change, and every deployment pulls approved changes on a daily schedule. Nothing scrapes government websites: no reliable official rates API exists, and a wrong compliance rate applied unattended costs more than a person checking around Budget day and GST Council meetings.

## How does bank reconciliation decide what to match?

A bank statement is imported from the bank's own export, and each line is matched against unreconciled ledger entries by exact amount within three days either side. A match is applied automatically only when it's mutually unique — exactly one candidate on each side. Anything ambiguous is shown as a suggestion for a person to confirm, and a statement line with no ledger entry at all — a bank charge, interest — becomes a one-click journal entry instead of a dead end.

## How was it tested?

With real transactions, not only unit tests. A reverse-charge test that posted real documents through the ledger found and fixed two posting bugs. A single order was then run through every department end to end, which found that sales invoices weren't carrying their project link — fixed before any real invoice depended on it.

## Boundary

[E-invoicing](/systems/e-invoice) has been researched and deliberately deferred. The system keeps one set of books per legal entity; consolidation across entities isn't built.

Where a business keeps its accounting software instead, the shop system posts to it: see [what QuickBooks does for manufacturing, and how a shop system sits beside it](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing).

title: AI extraction with a human in the loop, five document types
answer: Five document types — purchase invoices, freight invoices, bills of entry, purchase orders, bank statements — get extracted by an LLM reading the PDF directly, no separate OCR step. Zero-correction rates run 88-95% depending on type, purchase orders highest, bills of entry lowest. Every extraction still goes through a human review before anything is approved or posted.
body:
## What gets extracted

LS Technologies, an electronics-components import/export trading business, runs five kinds of documents through AI extraction before anything reaches Tally: purchase invoices, freight invoices, bills of entry, purchase orders, and bank statements. Each has its own prompt tailored to that document's fields — a purchase invoice and a customs bill of entry don't share a structure, and treating them as one generic "document" would lose accuracy on both.

## How it reads a PDF

There's no separate OCR step. The PDF is sent straight to the model — an LLM with a file-parsing capability reads it directly, rather than running text extraction first and handing the model plain text. Bank statements get special handling: because they can run to many pages, the document is processed in chunks and the results are stitched back together and de-duplicated, rather than trying to reason over one long document in a single pass.

## How accurate it actually is

Reviewed against real usage, here's the share of each document type that needs zero correction before it's approved:

- Purchase order: 95%
- Purchase invoice: 94%
- Bank statement: 89%
- Freight invoice: 91%
- Bill of entry: 88%

Bills of entry come in lowest — customs documentation is the least standardized of the five, which tracks with what you'd expect from the least uniform paperwork. Every number here still means a meaningful share of documents need a correction, which is exactly why extraction alone was never the plan.

## How do these numbers compare with advertised accuracy?

Invoice-automation tools commonly advertise 95–99% accuracy. A 2026 benchmark review found those claims have converged in that range while being measured under conditions each vendor chooses, with no independent benchmark behind them ([Parseur](https://parseur.com/blog/ai-invoice-processing-benchmarks)). The figures above are lower, and deliberately so: they're per document type, from real usage, and they count any document a person had to correct — including customs paperwork such as bills of entry. A lower number measured honestly is more useful for planning than a higher one measured on a vendor's own samples.

## What happens to the rest

Nothing gets extracted and posted in one step. Every document — regardless of how confident the extraction looked — sits in a review state until a person checks it and approves it. That's not a hedge against a bad model; it's the same decision this practice makes anywhere a model's output could turn into a financial record: draft with AI, confirm with a person, post only after that.

title: An assistant that only answers from your own records, and never invents a number
description: How the assistants in Ahrom Labs' client systems pick a fixed look-up instead of writing SQL or guessing, so every figure matches the screens.
answer: The assistants Ahrom Labs builds into client systems don't let a language model write the answer's numbers. A small decision model only chooses what kind of question it is, which look-up to run and for what period; ordinary code runs a fixed query using the same maths as the app's own screens. At Savistar and Saag it routed 55 of 55 test questions and 57 unseen real phrasings correctly, including Hinglish.

evidence.value: code — a fixed, parameterised look-up per question type, the same maths as the app's screens
the kind of question, the look-up, the company, the period, whether it's a follow-up
29, over clients, projects, quotations, orders, vendors, people, tasks, cash, the bank and money
55 of 55 test questions and 57 unseen real-world phrasings, with typos, fragments and Hinglish

evidence.metric: written answers with a number not in the data
evidence.value: dropped, checked by a script on every persona
only their own tasks and their own cash entries; payroll and bank statements refused

body:
An owner wants to ask "how did this month compare with last month?" and get the real answer, not a confident paragraph that's nearly right. A chatbot that writes SQL, or reads rows and summarises them, will sooner or later give a figure that doesn't match the accounts. In a business system, one wrong number is enough for nobody to trust it again. So the assistants in Ahrom Labs' client systems are built so the model never produces the number, the same rule as [AI document reading](/notes/ai-extraction-human-in-the-loop), where a person approves every document before it reaches the books.

## How does a question get answered?

In two steps, and only the first uses AI. A small decision model reads the question and picks from fixed options: what kind of question it is (data, how-to, a reminder, small talk, something it can't answer), which look-up fits, which company, which period, and whether it follows on from the last question. It returns a choice, not text. Then ordinary code matches names ("the Mehtas", "Shree Plywood") to real records and runs a fixed, parameterised query. The answer is a table built with the same maths as the app's own screens, so the assistant's revenue figure and the Finance tab's figure are the same figure.

At Savistar and Saag, an interior design studio and a furniture workshop sharing one system, there are 29 of these look-ups: projects due, late workshop orders, unpaid invoices, open quotations, who worked on what, vendor balances, attendance, bank balances, period comparisons and so on. Each one is listed, with the screen to check it against, in the [question library](/ai-assistant/interior-design-firms).

## Then where does the personality come from?

From an optional sentence above the table. Savistar's assistant, Atelier AI, lets each person pick a voice: plain, studio partner, site supervisor, finance desk or a gentler guide. The written line is checked before it's shown: if it contains any number that isn't in the table, it's dropped and only the table is shown. A script runs that check on every persona.

## What happens when it can't answer?

It says so. Questions about advice, or about data the system doesn't hold, get a plain "the data doesn't have that" and a few useful questions it can answer. Every miss and every thumbs-down is listed in Settings, so the next look-up to add comes from what people actually asked rather than a guess.

## Can it change anything?

No. Look-ups are read-only. "Remind me to call the Mehtas on Friday" drafts a task and "note that they prefer walnut" drafts a private note, but nothing is saved until the person presses Save. Staff can only ask about their own tasks and their own cash entries; payroll and bank statements are refused to them, the same way the screens refuse them.

## Is it the same assistant everywhere?

The design is the same; the assistant isn't. Each one is built on its own system's records and words. [Ohm AI](/ai-assistant/trading-distribution), LS Technologies' assistant, answers its own staff about reels, stores, customers and stock, with a daily question limit and a cost of about a hundredth of a rupee per question. [Ember AI](/ai-assistant/manufacturers), at the boiler manufacturer, starts with how-to questions from the help guide, without sending any business data out. Atelier AI, Savistar's, has the personas and notes. Each one is tested with its own question set, run through the real pipeline, before it goes live. To test any vendor's assistant the same way, there is a [question library](/ai-assistant/questions), a [vendor test](/ai-assistant/vendor-test) and a [check for made-up numbers](/ai-assistant/number-check); the design is laid out for buyers in [how it works](/ai-assistant/how-it-works), and what it sends out in [data safety](/ai-assistant/data-safety).

## Boundary

The decision model is a third-party model reached through OpenRouter, using the client's own key and a daily question limit. In Savistar's system, if it's unavailable a keyword router takes over: answers get less clever, but not wrong, because the numbers still come from the same look-ups.

title: Four ways to connect a business system to TallyPrime
answer: TallyPrime has no cloud API — its integration gateway only listens on the PC that runs it — so every connection is a bridge on that machine. Ahrom Labs has built four: a local agent that posts approved entries from a cloud database; the same agent hardened for offices whose internet drops; an MCP server that gives applications and AI agents one set of Tally tools; and a CSV or JSON export and import for when nothing can be installed.

evidence.value: 4 — local agent, hardened agent, MCP server, CSV/JSON files
30 seconds

evidence.metric: Voucher status and outstanding bills synced back
evidence.value: every 15 minutes
flagged for a person, never auto-created

body:
## Why can't a web app just call Tally?

Because TallyPrime doesn't expose anything to the internet. Its integration surface is an XML gateway that listens on the machine where Tally runs, inside the office network. A cloud-hosted app — an ERP, a CRM, an inventory system — can't reach it directly, so something on or next to that machine has to carry entries in and bring data back out. The four approaches below are the ones Ahrom Labs has built, in the order they came about, each one answering a problem the previous one exposed.

## 1. A local agent on the Tally PC

The first connection was a small agent running on the same PC as TallyPrime. The cloud app never talks to Tally: it writes to its own online database, and the agent reads approved entries from there and posts them into Tally's gateway. At [LS Technologies](/industries/electronics-component-trading) it picks up approved invoices every 30 seconds, syncs voucher status and outstanding bills back every 15 minutes, and refreshes ledgers, stock items and voucher types nightly. A ledger that doesn't exist yet in Tally is flagged for a person, never created by the software. The details are in [Posting vouchers into TallyPrime from a cloud app](/notes/tally-voucher-posting), and the XML protocol code is open-sourced as [tally-voucher-xml](https://github.com/Ahrom-Labs/tally-voucher-xml).

## 2. The same agent, hardened for a connection that drops

An agent that talks to a cloud database is only as good as the office's internet, and in practice that connection wasn't consistent. So the agent was made more robust around exactly that: every failure is classified before anything else happens. If Tally or the connection is simply unavailable, the entry stays queued and posts on a later cycle, with no restart and no person involved. If Tally actually rejects it — a missing ledger, a duplicate — it's held with the exact reason until someone fixes it. After each sync, the system checks what Tally really holds, so a voucher deleted inside Tally shows up as unconfirmed rather than silently assumed posted.

## 3. An MCP server in front of Tally

The newest connection is an MCP server that talks to Tally. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for exposing a system's operations as named tools that software and AI agents can call. Instead of every application learning Tally's XML on its own, each one — including an AI agent — reaches Tally through the same defined set of tools. It turns "integrate with Tally" from a per-project job into one shared piece of the accounting layer.

## 4. CSV and JSON export and import

Some situations can't run anything automatic: the Tally PC isn't always on, nothing can be installed on it yet, or the accountant wants to see and control every import. For those, the connection is a file. Entries are downloaded from the business system as CSV or JSON and brought into Tally, and data exported from Tally is uploaded back the same way. It's slower and manual, but it works everywhere and it keeps the accountant in charge of exactly what enters the books.

## Which one should a business use?

- **Tally stays the books, the PC is on during working hours, and entries should flow on their own** — the local agent.
- **Several applications, or AI agents, need to read from or post to Tally** — the MCP server, so they share one connection instead of each building its own.
- **A first step, an occasional sync, or an accountant who wants control** — file export and import.
- **Most of the accounting starts as operational events** — sometimes the better answer is to keep the books inside the operations system and make Tally optional, as [one boiler manufacturer](/notes/accounting-inside-the-manufacturing-erp) did.

These aren't exclusive. The file path remains the fallback whichever live connection a business uses.

## Boundary

Every live connection needs the machine running Tally to be switched on; if it's off, nothing moves until it's back. File export and import is only as current as the last file. None of this is a cloud-to-cloud integration, because TallyPrime doesn't offer one. TallyPrime is a product of Tally Solutions; Ahrom Labs isn't affiliated with it.

title: What a customer sees: one boiler order through every department
description: How a manufacturer's customers follow their own order, approve drawings and download documents, from the same records the factory works in.
answer: At a boiler manufacturer Ahrom Labs built for, each customer gets a login that shows their orders as nine plain-language stages, from Order Received to Commissioning, worked out from the same records each department already keeps. Customers approve drawings, upload their own, download QC certificates, packing lists and invoices, and request quotes, without phoning anyone to ask.

evidence.value: 9 — Order Received, Design & Engineering, Material Procurement, Manufacturing, Quality Testing, Documentation, Packing, Site Installation, Commissioning

evidence.metric: where each stage's status comes from
evidence.value: the department's own records (job card stages, QC sign-off, documents shared, packing lists dispatched), never a status someone types for the customer
approve drawings, upload their own drawings, download QC certificates, packing lists and invoices, request a quote from the product range
other customers' orders, notes between departments, internal costs
LS Technologies — each line of a customer PO with its status and progress, no stock figures, suppliers or costs

body:
A customer who has ordered a boiler waits months for it, and in that time they ring the sales engineer to ask where it is. The sales engineer rings Production, Production checks with Stores, and the answer comes back a day later, already out of date. At one boiler and pressure-vessel manufacturer, the operations system Ahrom Labs built now answers that question directly, to the customer, from the same records the factory works in.

## What does the customer actually see?

Each customer company gets one login, and a My Orders page with every order they have placed. Opening an order shows nine stages in the customer's language, not the factory's: Order Received, Design & Engineering, Material Procurement, Manufacturing, Quality Testing, Documentation, Packing, Site Installation and Commissioning. Each stage shows whether it's done, in progress or not started, with the overall percentage and the expected dispatch date. An "About your order" button explains each stage in plain words.

Documents sit under the stage they belong to: drawings under Design & Engineering, test certificates under Quality Testing, packing lists under Packing. Invoices sit in their own Billing section, because an invoice can be raised at booking, midway or at dispatch, and pinning it to one stage would be made up.

## Where does the status come from?

Nobody types a status for the customer. Each stage reads the department's own work: Manufacturing is done when the job card stages are finished, Quality Testing when QC has signed the same stages off, Documentation when every statutory document is complete and shared, Packing when the packing lists have left. If Production is behind, the portal is behind too. That's the point: the customer sees the truth, and the factory doesn't keep a second, friendlier version of it.

When part of an order has shipped and the rest hasn't, the portal says so ("14 of 168 items sent") with a list the customer can download.

## What can the customer do, not just read?

Drawings are shared by the Design Head one at a time, and only when they're ready. The customer approves each one, and their name and the date appear on it. When every shared drawing is approved, the Design Approval milestone completes by itself. Customers can also upload their own drawings and site layouts, so they don't arrive by email and get lost.

Every document downloads as the same PDF the factory files. The nameplate on each finished unit carries a QR sticker that opens the order in the portal, so years later the documents are still one scan away. Signed-in customers can also browse the product range and request a quote, which reaches Sales as an enquiry, linked to the customer.

## What stays private?

A customer only ever sees their own orders. Every page and download checks that the order belongs to that login. Nothing internal is shown: no internal costs, no notes between departments, no stock figures. Logins are created by Sales for each customer; the customer sets their own password from a one-time link, so no password is ever emailed.

## Is this only for manufacturers?

The same idea runs at LS Technologies, an electronics component trader. Their customers see each line of a purchase order with its status (ordered, reserved, in procurement, dispatched) and a progress bar, without seeing stock figures, suppliers or costs. A partner store that holds LS stock buys through the same portal; [how LS tracks and reserves that stock](/notes/reels-boxes-and-two-stores) is its own note.

## Boundary

The portal is read-mostly. Customers approve, upload and request quotes; they don't edit orders, prices or dates. Status emails go out through the manufacturer's own mailbox, which they switch on per customer.

title: Keeping test certificates for a boiler's IBR folder
answer: A boiler manufacturer ships every boiler with an IBR statutory folder for the Directorate of Boilers. The system produces it — cover letter, Forms II(1), III, III A and IV A (under IBR 2026: Forms I Part B, IV Part A, IV Part B and V Part B) — from a bank of material test certificates, each unique on cert, cast and plate number and reused across about 3.2 boilers in the sample. The form set follows the boiler model; a person adds the parts, so a folder takes a few minutes instead of being typed up by hand.

evidence.value: cert no. + cast no. + plate no. together — one cert number covered 4 casts in the sample
about 3.2 boilers per certificate in the real sample
chosen by boiler model — 8 models, each with its own set

evidence.metric: adding a boiler's parts to the folder
evidence.value: a few minutes, by a person; the BOM alone doesn't fill the forms reliably
suggested by confidence, never applied without a person

body:
The manufacturer this was built for makes boilers, pressure-reducing stations and steam headers. Every unit it ships needs a [statutory folder](/systems/ibr-statutory-folder) for the Directorate of Boilers, under the Indian Boiler Regulations (IBR): the forms that prove each plate, tube and forging came from certified material. Ahrom Labs built the operations system that now keeps the certificates and produces that folder.

## What goes into the folder?

The folder described here was filed under the Indian Boiler Regulations, 1950, so it uses their form names. IBR 2026 renumbered them on 1 October 2026: Form II(1) is now Form I Part B, Form III is Form IV Part A, Form III A is Form IV Part B, Form IV A is Form V Part B and Form XVII is Form XXII. See [the IBR 2026 forms list](/ibr/forms).

A complete folder is filed in a fixed order: a covering letter listing its contents, a documentation label, the forms, the list of mountings and fittings, a stage-wise inspection report, and copies of the [material test certificates](/systems/material-test-certificate) themselves. Which forms are needed depends on the boiler model — a standard shell boiler needs Form II(1), III, III A and IV A; a small industrial boiler swaps II(1) and III for Form XVII; a pressure-reducing station or steam header needs only III and IV A. The system picks the form set from the model set on the project, not from a person remembering which applies.

## Why is a test certificate harder to key than it looks?

A certificate number alone isn't unique — in the client's own sample, one certificate number covered four different casts. So each certificate in the bank is identified by certificate number, cast number and plate number together. And one certificate isn't used once: a single plate gets cut into parts for several boilers, and the sample showed each certificate reused across about 3.2 of them. Certificates and projects are therefore many-to-many — a certificate can be uploaded before any project claims it, and using it on a project's folder is what allocates it.

## Why does a person add the parts?

Form IV A lists every material part with its certificate, grouped into lettered sections — A. Shell, B. Water Wall Assembly, and so on. The bill of materials a plant keeps for buying and production isn't shaped like that form, and building the form from it alone wasn't reliable enough for paperwork an inspector relies on. So a person adds the parts to the folder and picks each one's certificate from the bank; for a boiler that takes a few minutes. Anything not yet placed lands on a clearly labelled "Ungrouped Materials" page rather than disappearing.

## Where does AI help, and where does it stop?

Certificate PDFs are read by AI on upload, so the certificate's fields don't have to be typed. Matching a certificate to the part it covers is suggested by a confidence score learned from past approvals — but on this document, a suggestion never links itself. A person clicks to use it, because a wrong link here ends up in paperwork a boiler inspector relies on. The [same-confidence note](/notes/same-confidence-different-autonomy) explains why the identical score is allowed to act on its own elsewhere in the same system.

The ASME Code asks for the same trail behind its Manufacturer's Data Report, the document an ASME-stamped boiler or vessel ships with; see [ASME data reports](/asme/data-reports) and [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## Boundary

The folder the system produces has been compared against real filed documents the client provided. That comparison found formatting gaps in individual forms — wording and field-layout differences — which are tracked and being closed form by form. Bulk import of historical certificates from spreadsheets isn't built yet; certificates are added one at a time, with AI filling the fields.

title: Seven signs your business has outgrown Tally — and what fixed each one
answer: You've outgrown Tally when the work happens outside it: invoices typed twice, a parallel Excel for production, sales asking accounts for outstanding balances, stock Tally can't describe. Replacing Tally is rarely the fix — in one system we built, Tally stays as the books and approved invoices post into it within 30 seconds.

evidence.value: within 30 seconds, through a local agent

evidence.metric: Outstanding balances back to the sales side
evidence.value: every 15 minutes

evidence.metric: Import documents read by AI instead of typed
evidence.value: 5 types, 88–95% needing no correction

body:
TallyPrime is excellent at what it's for: the books. Businesses outgrow it not because it gets worse, but because more of their work happens somewhere Tally can't see. Here are the seven signs we see most — each one drawn from a business we've built for, with what fixed it.

## 1. The same invoice is typed twice

Once into a spreadsheet or web app for operations, once into Tally for accounts. At [LS Technologies](/industries/electronics-component-trading), an electronics importer, approved invoices now post into Tally as vouchers within 30 seconds through a small agent on the Tally PC — no second typing. See [Posting vouchers into TallyPrime from a cloud app](/notes/tally-voucher-posting).

## 2. Someone reads every PDF and keys it in

Purchase invoices, freight bills, bills of entry, bank statements. At the same business, AI reads five document types directly from the PDF, and 88–95% need no correction depending on type — but every one is still approved by a person before it posts. See [AI extraction with a human in the loop](/notes/ai-extraction-human-in-the-loop).

## 3. Sales keeps asking accounts what a customer owes

Outstanding balances live in Tally; the sales team doesn't. The fix is syncing them back: in the same system, voucher status and outstanding bills flow from Tally to the sales side every 15 minutes.

## 4. Production runs on a parallel Excel

Work orders, job cards, material issues, what's waiting on what — none of it fits vouchers. At [a boiler manufacturer](/industries/boiler-pressure-vessel-manufacturing), each boiler is a project with its own bill of materials and milestones across design, procurement, stores, production, QC and dispatch, and the system shows what each step is waiting on.

## 5. Your stock isn't really a count

Steel plate gets cut; the offcut is a specific piece, not "one more plate". Reels of components move between locations. Tally stores quantities. In the system built for that manufacturer, every plate is a piece with dimensions and every cut is recorded, so a 15.70 kg remnant goes back into stock instead of being scrapped. See [Putting steel plate offcuts back into stock](/notes/plate-remnants-back-into-stock).

## 6. Two companies, one owner, one office

A design firm and its furniture workshop; a trading firm and its sister concern. Two sets of books, one client list, and staff who need to record cash without seeing the bank. At [Savistar and Saag](/industries/interior-design-and-furniture), both run on one system: each invoice carries its own company's GSTIN, and staff see only their own cash entries. See [Two companies, one book](/notes/two-companies-one-book).

## 7. Industry paperwork is assembled by hand

A boiler's [statutory folder](/systems/ibr-statutory-folder), a test-certificate trail, a customs file. If a person compiles it from records that already exist in your systems, it can be generated instead — as that manufacturer's IBR folder now is. See [Generating a boiler's IBR statutory folder](/notes/ibr-statutory-folder-from-bom).

## Do you have to replace Tally?

Usually not. There are two sound paths. Keep Tally as the books and connect an operations system to it, as LS Technologies did — the accountant's workflow doesn't change. Or move the books into the operations system and keep Tally as an optional sync, as the boiler manufacturer did. Which one fits depends on how much of your accounting starts as operational events. The [comparison of Tally, ERPNext, Odoo and custom](/notes/tally-vs-erpnext-vs-custom-erp) covers the choice in full.

When it's time to write down what the next system must do, start from the [ERP requirements checklist](/erp/requirements), or let the [requirements builder](/erp/check) pick the lines that apply to your business.

## Boundary

These signs come from three businesses — trading, manufacturing, interior design. If only one or two apply, a smaller fix (an integration, a report) may be enough; that's worth finding out before building anything.

title: Putting steel plate offcuts back into stock, by weight derived from geometry
answer: At a boiler manufacturer Ahrom Labs built for, every cut of a plate or section records what was used and what usable remnant was kept; the system derives every weight from dimensions and density, returns the remnant to stock for a later project, and books the rest as scrap. A 157.00 kg plate became 127.17 kg used, 15.70 kg remnant and 14.13 kg scrap — conserved exactly.

evidence.value: 157.00 kg source → 127.17 kg used + 15.70 kg remnant + 14.13 kg scrap
none — plate L×W×T×density, sections length×kg/m
every cut output chained to its source piece (used, remnant, scrap)
by weight fraction — 100 kg used of a 157 kg, ₹1,000 plate → ₹636.94

body:
A boiler maker buys steel plate in standard sizes and cuts it to the parts a design needs. The leftover is often big enough to use on the next job — if anyone knows it exists. At one boiler and pressure-vessel manufacturer, it used to be re-bought or scrapped blindly. This is how the operations system Ahrom Labs built now keeps it.

## Why couldn't the old stock record hold an offcut?

Inventory was a single number per item — how many plates of a grade and size were on hand. An offcut isn't one of those plates; it's a specific piece with its own dimensions. With nowhere to record a piece, a remnant sitting in the stores could never be matched to a future bill of materials, even when it was exactly the right size.

## What gets recorded at the moment of cutting?

Each physical piece carries its own dimensions: length, width and thickness for a plate; length and weight-per-metre for an angle, channel, beam, pipe or bar. At the cut, the operator enters only what was used and what usable remnant they kept. The source piece is closed, each used piece is linked to the project it went into, each remnant goes back into stock as an available piece, and whatever weight is left over is booked as scrap automatically. Every output is chained to the piece it came from, so a part on a finished boiler traces back to the plate it was cut from.

## Why derive weight instead of weighing or typing it?

Weight is computed from geometry and density — never typed. That makes the arithmetic self-checking: used plus remnant plus scrap must equal the source. In the live test, a 2000 × 1000 × 10 mm plate (157.00 kg) was cut into a 127.17 kg part and a 15.70 kg remnant, leaving 14.13 kg of scrap — summing exactly back to the source. A typed weight can't be held to that standard; a derived one can't fail it.

## How does a remnant get reused?

Because a remnant is stored as a real piece with real dimensions, it's matched against bill-of-materials lines still waiting for material, exactly like a newly purchased plate. When a BOM is released, a fitting piece is reserved automatically — the least-waste piece first, a thickness mismatch rejected, rotation allowed so an offcut that fits sideways still counts — and only the shortfall goes to Procurement to buy. In the live test, a line needing two pieces with one matching remnant in stock reserved that remnant and sent only the second piece to purchasing.

## What does a cut piece cost?

Cost follows weight. A used piece carries the fraction of its source's cost that its weight represents: 100 kg used from a 157 kg plate that cost ₹1,000 is booked at ₹636.94. Building this surfaced a real, pre-existing error in how average cost was being recalculated for piece-tracked stock — fixed at the root rather than patched in the report.

The ASME Code puts the same requirement in its rule on transferring material markings when plate is cut (UG-77); see [material test reports and heat numbers](/asme/mtr).

## Boundary

Piece tracking is switched on per item and applies to plate and section stock that's actually cut. Matching looks for one sufficient piece per requirement; nesting — planning the most economical 2D layout of several parts on one plate before cutting — is not part of this system.

title: Reels, boxes and two stores — stock you can scan and set aside for each order
description: How LS Technologies tracks every component reel by QR across two stores, and reserves stock for each customer order before it ships.
answer: For LS Technologies, an electronic components trader, Ahrom Labs built an inventory system where every reel and box carries a QR label, stock moves by scanning from a phone, and staff entries wait for a manager's approval. Stock is held in two stores, the second at a partner's site, and whole reels are reserved against each customer order line before they ship. 5,256 live reels moved to the two-store model with none lost.

scan with a phone camera or scanner into a cart; inward, outward and store-to-store transfer
queued for a manager to approve, edit or reject; managers' own entries go through at once

evidence.metric: live reels moved to two stores
evidence.value: 5,256, every one checked after the change

body:
An electronics trader's stock isn't "500 of part X". It's reels, each holding a different quantity of one part, packed in boxes, sitting on shelves in more than one place. LS Technologies used to know roughly what it had. The system Ahrom Labs built for them knows each reel.

## Why track reels, not quantities?

Because customers order quantities, but the store ships reels. Two reels of the same part, one of 5,000 and one of 1,200, aren't interchangeable when an order needs 5,000. So each reel gets its own number and QR label when it's received, printed on the spot, and reels are grouped into boxes with their own labels. The quantity in stock is worked out from the reels, never kept as a separate number that could drift.

## How does stock move?

By scanning. On the Outward screen, a store hand scans reels or whole boxes with a phone camera or a scanner into a cart, picks the customer and their purchase order, and submits. The packing list prints from the same cart. Receiving and moving stock between stores work the same way. Part of a reel can ship and the rest stays in stock with its new quantity.

Staff entries don't change stock directly. They go to a manager, who approves, edits or rejects them; managers' own entries go through at once. Every entry can be undone by a manager, and an undo restores exactly that reel.

## What changed with a second store?

LS keeps stock at a partner's site too. Each reel now records which store it's in, every store-to-store move is logged reel by reel, and the screens filter by store. The change was made on the live database: 5,256 reels moved to the two-store model, every one checked afterwards.

The partner's own staff see only their store. Before they can record anything each day, their manager approves the previous day's outgoing summary, so the partner's movements are reviewed daily instead of line by line. Shipments from the partner store get a tax invoice in the same number series LS uses in Tally.

One real incident shaped the rules. A shipment was once recorded against the wrong store because a dropdown had been left on the other store. Now a shipment always takes the store the reel is actually in; the screen can't override it.

## How is stock kept for a customer?

A customer's purchase order line can reserve whole reels, oldest stock first, until the line is covered. A reserved reel shows as reserved when scanned, and shipping it to anyone else needs a manager's override. When stock doesn't cover the open orders, the shortfall is pooled by part into a procurement order, including imports, tracked through its own stages to Received. Reels received against it are reserved to the waiting orders automatically, earliest dispatch date first.

Customers see each line of their order as reserved, in procurement or dispatched, with a progress bar, through their own login, without seeing stock figures, suppliers or costs. A boiler manufacturer's [customer portal](/notes/customer-portal-one-order-every-department) works the same way, from its own records.

## Boundary

Reservations hold whole reels, so the last reel can cover more than the line needs. Stock in the partner store never counts as free stock for LS's own orders.

Why a stock layer like this sits beside accounting software rather than inside it: [QuickBooks Online inventory and where manufacturers outgrow it](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory).

title: Moving five years of sales history into one CRM, without guessing a single customer
description: How a manufacturer's old CRM diary, quotation register and Excel order tracker moved into one sales system, with every doubtful row held for review.
answer: At a boiler manufacturer Ahrom Labs built for, sales history lived in an old CRM and an Excel tracker. Moving it in recovered all 20,167 diary rows, including 154 that a broken export had shifted, imported 2,221 quotations that matched exactly one customer and 1,006 orders with 1,905 payments, and held 303 doubtful quotations for a person instead of guessing.

evidence.value: 1,006 orders and 1,905 payments, five financial years

body:
A sales team's memory is its history: who asked for what, what was quoted, what was promised on the last call. At one boiler and pressure-vessel manufacturer, that history sat in three places: an old CRM's diary, the same CRM's quotation register, and an Excel sheet tracking every order and payment. The operations system Ahrom Labs built needed all of it in one place, so a salesperson opening a customer sees everything that customer has ever asked for.

## Why not just import the files?

Because an export is never as clean as it looks, and a CRM that starts with wrong history is worse than one that starts empty. Every file was checked against itself before anything was loaded.

The diary export had 20,167 rows. In 154 of them (0.76%), a contact address written over several lines had pushed the later columns one or two places to the right, so a naive read by column name lost the real status off the end of the row. The importer finds those rows from their known last columns and reads them correctly. All 20,167 rows were recovered.

## Why import fewer notes than rows?

Because the old CRM repeated one note on every row for an organisation: one customer had the same note on 135 rows spanning a year. Importing row by row would have filled each customer's history with copies. Collapsed to distinct notes, the 20,167 rows became 2,199 real notes, each attached to the customer it belongs to. 214 organisations had rows but no note text ever written; they were skipped rather than given a made-up placeholder.

## What happens to a quotation that matches two customers?

It waits for a person. The quotation register named customers the way people type them, so "ABC Industries" and "A.B.C. Industries Pvt Ltd" could be the same company or two. 2,221 quotations (counting revisions) matched exactly one customer and were imported. 303 matched none, or more than one, and went into a review list instead. A quotation attached to the wrong customer would show up in someone's history as something they never asked for.

The order tracker, kept in Excel for five financial years, came in the same way: 1,006 orders and 1,905 payments, every row tagged with the import it came from so it can be removed as one batch if anything is ever found wrong.

## What does the sales team get?

One place for every enquiry. The funnel stage is an enquiry's only status, with its history, so nothing is "open" in one screen and "lost" in another. A follow-up diary and a weekly planner show who should call whom this week. Quotations go out as PDFs in the company's own format, with its terms, GST and the amount in words, and they can be revised without starting again. Product prices keep their history. Order and payment tracking, win/loss, funnel ageing and salesperson reports read the same records, and once an order is placed the customer follows it through [their own portal](/notes/customer-portal-one-order-every-department).

Connections to IndiaMART, TradeIndia, JustDial and website forms are built: each enquiry lands in Sales, assigned in turn, the moment the company adds its own key.

## Boundary

The old quotation register held only headers (number, date, customer, status), no line items or prices, so imported quotations show when and to whom, not what. New quotations carry their full lines.

title: The same confidence score, two different autonomy rules
answer: Two match-suggestion systems in the same manufacturing app score candidates identically — a Laplace-smoothed approval ratio, promoted at 75% confidence with at least 3 prior approvals. One auto-applies its top match. The other never does, no matter how confident the score, because it decides what goes on a statutory quality-control document.

evidence.value: (approvals+1) / (approvals+rejections+2) ≥ 0.75, minimum 3 approvals
never auto-applies — a person always clicks "use this certificate"
auto-reserves its top match, same confidence math, same threshold

body:
## Two systems, the same scoring math

A manufacturing operation runs two independent match-suggestion systems that solve the same shape of problem: given a new record, rank the best existing candidates to link it to. Both score confidence the same way — a Laplace-smoothed approval ratio, `(approvals + 1) / (approvals + rejections + 2)`, promoted to "high confidence" once it clears 0.75 with at least 3 recorded approvals.

## What each one is actually matching

One system matches leftover cut material back to bill-of-materials lines still waiting on stock — reserving whichever offcut fits, rotation allowed, so usable material doesn't get set aside as scrap. The other matches incoming test certificates to the bill-of-materials line they belong to, the record that ends up inside a statutory quality-control document.

## Same score, different action

At the identical confidence threshold, the stock-matching system auto-reserves its top candidate the moment it clears the bar — a database write happens with no person involved. The certificate-matching system never does that. It always returns a ranked list; nothing gets linked until a person clicks "use this certificate." A promoted, high-confidence match just moves to the top of that list — it doesn't get to act on its own.

## Why the same math earns different trust

A wrong [stock reservation](/systems/stock-reservation) is a wasted click — someone notices the piece doesn't fit and picks another from the list. A wrong match on a quality certificate becomes part of the paperwork proving a part meets its material specification. The statistics can't tell those two mistakes apart; the decision about which one gets to act unsupervised has to be made separately, by someone who understands what's actually at stake on each side.

title: Keeping GST, TDS and income-tax rates current across every system
answer: Ahrom Labs keeps statutory rates — GST by HSN code, vendor TDS, income-tax and professional-tax slabs, PF and ESI — in one registry built to serve every system it builds, with a boiler manufacturer's system the first connected. A person checks each change against the actual CBIC or CBDT notification, a change goes live only once approved, installs pull approved rates daily, and a wrong rate is retracted rather than edited.

evidence.value: GST by HSN, vendor TDS, income-tax slabs, professional-tax slabs, PF/ESI
Draft, then approved by a person; never applied unapproved
Daily, 02:00 IST
Retracted with a reason; the original and its approval kept

body:
## Why not fetch tax rates automatically?

Because there is nothing reliable to fetch from. When this registry was built, the sources were checked one by one: no government API publishes GST, TDS or income-tax rates in a machine-readable, effective-dated form, and the commercial compliance APIs checked offered filing, calculators and GSTIN lookup — not a rate feed. Scraping notification pages works until the day a page changes shape, and then it fails silently. For a number that ends up on invoices and in returns, being wrong unattended costs more than being a few days late. Rates change on mostly predictable occasions — the Union Budget, GST Council meetings, state notifications — so a person checking a few times a year is cheap and reliable.

## How does a rate change reach every system?

1. Someone reads the actual CBIC or CBDT notification and records the change in the registry's dataset.
2. A daily job compares the dataset against every version already recorded. Unchanged data does nothing; a new or changed rate becomes a draft; a conflicting value for the same effective date is rejected rather than drafted. An approved rate is never overwritten.
3. A person reviews the drafts and approves them — one at a time or in bulk.
4. Each connected system pulls approved changes on its own daily schedule, using a cursor so nothing is missed or pulled twice, and applies them through the same insert and validation it uses when someone types a rate in by hand.

Each system has its own key, so the registry knows who is pulling and a new installation is one key away from receiving every verified rate.

## What happens when an approved rate turns out to be wrong?

It's retracted, not edited. The original row and the record of who approved it stay in the registry permanently, a reason is required, a corrected replacement is drafted and approved separately, and the retracted row is never served again. The history of what a system believed, and when, survives the correction — which matters when someone later asks why an invoice carried the rate it did.

## How do you know the sync is still running?

The registry's daily refresh runs at 02:00 IST, half an hour before the connected systems pull, so they always pull after it has finished. Every run records a heartbeat — running, then success or failure — visible at the top of the registry's admin screen. The scheduled trigger also reports to an external check that sends an email if the schedule itself stops firing, because a job that never runs can't report its own failure.

## What else sits in the compliance core?

The rates registry is one part of the accounting and compliance layer that Ahrom Labs builds systems on:

- **GSTIN verification** — a live lookup of a customer's or vendor's GSTIN before it's saved.
- **GST returns** — GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B from the system's own ledger, and the government's GSTR-2B imported from the portal's download, with each line's Invoice Management System status — accepted, rejected, pending or deemed accepted — recorded against it. See [GST, TDS and the general ledger inside a manufacturing ERP](/notes/accounting-inside-the-manufacturing-erp).
- **[E-way bills](/systems/e-way-bill)** — a client that talks directly to the government's NIC e-way bill system, with no intermediary, built to the official v1.03 specification to generate and cancel e-way bills from the invoice's own line items. It is built and checked locally; it goes live once the company's NIC account is set up.
- **TallyPrime** — connected four ways, or made optional. See [Four ways to connect a business system to TallyPrime](/notes/connecting-tallyprime-four-ways).

## Boundary

Rates are only as current as the person maintaining the registry, so an unscheduled notification can take a short while to arrive — accepted in exchange for never applying an unverified rate. The registry stores rates; it doesn't decide which rate applies to a transaction or give tax advice, and a business's own CA remains the authority on its filings. A boiler manufacturer's system is the first connected; others connect as they need it.

title: Suppliers quote on a link, not a login, and see their PO when it's issued
description: How a manufacturer's suppliers quote, see the PO and record dispatch through one private link, while conversations stay on WhatsApp and phone.
answer: At a boiler manufacturer Ahrom Labs built for, each supplier gets one private link per request for quotation, sent on WhatsApp or email. They enter their rates there with no account to create, see whether they were chosen, then download the PO and record each dispatch with its LR number and photos. Stores sees the goods as on the way before the truck arrives.

evidence.metric: what a supplier needs to quote
evidence.value: the link — no login, no account, no app
WhatsApp, email or copied, from the RFQ screen; conversations stay where they already happen
the buyer who raised the RFQ is alerted; quotes compared side by side; choosing one drafts the PO
the same link shows the PO copy and a form to record each dispatch (lines and quantities, transporter, vehicle, LR number, up to 3 photos or PDFs)
the PO line marked On the way, with the LR number and transporter, before the goods arrive

body:
Buying for a boiler means hundreds of lines (plates, tubes, valves, fittings), each quoted by two or three suppliers. At one boiler and pressure-vessel manufacturer, that used to mean quotes arriving as WhatsApp photos, PDFs and phone calls, typed into a spreadsheet by the buyer to compare them, and then a round of calls to ask whether the material had left. The operations system Ahrom Labs built changed where the numbers land, not how people talk.

## Why a link and not a supplier portal?

Suppliers won't create an account and remember a password for every customer they sell to. A portal they have to log in to stays empty. So each supplier gets a private link per request for quotation. The buyer picks the lines and the suppliers, and the system sends each supplier their own link by WhatsApp or email, or the buyer copies it into a chat. The supplier opens it on their phone, enters a rate and delivery date per line, and submits. Nothing to install, nothing to sign up for.

Conversations stay where they already happen. The buyer still calls and still messages on WhatsApp. The system is built around the way this manufacturer already works with its suppliers, not the other way round. What changes is that the rates arrive as data, against the right line, instead of in a photo.

## What happens when quotes come in?

The buyer who raised the request is alerted as each one arrives. Procurement sees the quotes for each line side by side and picks a supplier. Picking one drafts the purchase order, so nothing is typed twice. A request can be edited after it's sent: suppliers added, a supplier who hasn't quoted removed, a line taken out.

## What does the supplier see after that?

Their link tells them whether they were chosen. Once the PO is issued, the same link shows their copy of the PO as a PDF and a form to record each dispatch: which lines and how much are on the truck (part shipments allowed, never more than is left), the transporter, vehicle, LR number and date, and up to three photos or PDFs of the bill or the loaded truck.

## What does the factory get from that?

Stores and Procurement are alerted when a supplier dispatches. The lines move to "in transit", and on the Stores receiving screen they show "On the way" with the LR number, transporter and a tracking link where one exists. When the truck arrives, Stores receives against lines it already knows are coming. Once goods have been received from a dispatch, the supplier can no longer change it, so the record of what was sent matches what came in.

## Boundary

Live tracking of the truck isn't part of this: the system stores the carrier's details, not its location. Suppliers can't see other suppliers' rates, other POs or anything beyond their own link. The same manufacturer's own customers follow their orders through [a portal of their own](/notes/customer-portal-one-order-every-department).

title: Posting vouchers into TallyPrime from a cloud app
