body:
## The two-year cycle

ASME revises the Code continuously in committee and publishes all the changes together every two years, in odd years. There are no addenda between editions any more: the cycle replaced them. Each edition becomes mandatory six months after it's published, which gives shops time to update procedures and their QC manual.

| Edition | Published | Mandatory |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 1 July 2023 | 1 January 2024 |
| 2025 | 1 July 2025 | 1 January 2026 |
| 2027 | Due July 2027 | Six months after |

The National Board applied the same date to data report forms: items built to the 2025 Code must use the 2025 forms, and reports on outdated forms are sent back. See [data reports](/asme/data-reports).

## Which edition applies to a vessel

The edition is fixed per job, not per day. In general, a vessel is built to the edition agreed for it (usually the one mandatory when the contract was signed), and the jurisdiction where it will be installed may require a particular one. Write the edition into the purchase order and the design basis, and make sure the QC manual tells staff how a job's edition is recorded.

Welding qualifications don't expire with an edition: a PQR or WPQ qualified under an earlier edition stays valid, and new qualifications follow the edition in force when they are made. The [Section IX guide](/asme/section-ix) covers the 2025 changes.

## Code cases

A **code case** is an approved alternative or addition published between editions: a new material, a new method, a relaxation in a defined situation. Using one is optional, needs the jurisdiction's acceptance, and must be recorded on the data report. Many are later written into the Code itself; some are annulled.

## Interpretations

An **interpretation** is ASME's written answer to a question about what the Code says. It isn't a change to the Code, and it doesn't approve a design; it tells you how the committee reads a paragraph. Interpretations are published by ASME and searchable online.

## Owning the Code

A certificate holder must own current editions of the sections its scope uses, bought from ASME or a licensed reseller. That's also why these guides cite paragraph numbers instead of reprinting them; see [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps) and [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

title: Essential and nonessential variables in ASME Section IX
question: What are essential variables in ASME welding?
answer: ASME Section IX classifies each welding variable. Changing an essential variable, such as the base metal P-number, filler F-number, thickness range or heat treatment, needs a new PQR. Supplementary essential variables count only when impact testing is required. Nonessential variables, such as groove design, can change by revising the WPS.
description: ASME Section IX essential, supplementary essential and nonessential variables explained, with common examples for procedures and for welders.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section IX: Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications)

body:
## Why variables are classified

A procedure test proves one set of conditions. Section IX's variable tables (QW-250 onwards, one per process) say which conditions matter to the weld's mechanical properties and how far you can move from the test before you have to test again.

## The three kinds, for procedures

| Kind | If you change it beyond the PQR | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| Essential | Qualify a new PQR | Base metal P-number; filler metal F-number and A-number; thickness beyond the qualified range; adding or removing post-weld heat treatment; a drop in preheat of more than 100 °F (56 °C); a change of process; adding or removing shielding gas or a backing gas in some processes |
| Supplementary essential | New PQR only if the construction code requires impact testing | Group number within a P-number; heat input increase; single to multi-pass changes in some processes |
| Nonessential | Revise the WPS; no new test | Groove design, backing type, technique details, cleaning methods |

The exact list differs for each process (SMAW, GTAW, GMAW, SAW, FCAW), so always read the table for the process on your WPS.

## Thickness ranges

A groove weld PQR qualifies a range of base metal thickness and of weld metal thickness based on the coupon's thickness. As a general picture, a coupon of moderate thickness qualifies from a minimum up to twice its thickness, with thicker coupons qualifying up to the maximum allowed. Where impact testing applies, the lower limit changes too. Section IX's thickness table (QW-451) gives the numbers.

## For welders

Welders have their own essential variables (QW-350 onwards): process, position, backing, the F-number of the filler, and diameter and thickness ranges. Changing one beyond the WPQ means a new welder test. See [welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification).

## Practical rules

- Keep a **PQR register** with each PQR's qualified ranges worked out once. Most WPS errors are ranges copied wrong.
- When a WPS cites two PQRs (for example to cover two thickness ranges), make sure every essential variable is covered by at least one.
- Impact-tested work is where supplementary essentials catch shops out. See [MDMT and impact testing](/asme/impact-testing).

The documents themselves are explained in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq), and the material grouping in [P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers](/asme/p-numbers).

title: Pressure vessel heads (UG-32): ellipsoidal vs torispherical
question: What is a 2:1 ellipsoidal head?
answer: A 2:1 ellipsoidal head is half an ellipse in section, its depth a quarter of its diameter, and it needs about the same thickness as the shell it closes. Torispherical (flanged and dished) heads are shallower and cheaper but thicker; hemispherical heads are the deepest and need about half the shell thickness. ASME UG-32 gives a formula for each.
description: ASME UG-32 formed heads compared: 2:1 ellipsoidal, torispherical (F&D, ASME 80-10) and hemispherical, with their thickness formulas and when to use each.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## The three common formed heads

| Head | Shape | Thickness (UG-32), internal pressure | Relative thickness | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2:1 ellipsoidal | Depth = D/4 | t = PD / (2SE − 0.2P) | About the shell's | The default for most vessels |
| Torispherical (standard "ASME F&D": crown radius about equal to the diameter, knuckle radius 6% of the crown radius) | Shallower, a spherical crown with a knuckle | t = 0.885PL / (SE − 0.1P) | Thicker than the shell | Low pressure, storage, where height matters |
| Hemispherical | Half a sphere | t = PL / (2SE − 0.2P) | About half the shell's | High pressure, large diameters |

D is the inside diameter, L the inside crown (or sphere) radius, and P, S and E are as in the [shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) guide. Each formula has validity limits, and other proportions (other ellipses, other crown and knuckle radii) use the general rules in Mandatory Appendix 1-4.

## Choosing

- **Cost**: a hemispherical head is the thinnest but the hardest to form and the deepest; torispherical heads are the cheapest to form but the thickest. The 2:1 ellipsoidal sits between and is the usual answer.
- **Height and volume**: torispherical heads save height; hemispherical heads add the most volume.
- **Joint efficiency**: a seamless head's E depends on the radiography of the weld that joins it to the shell; see [joint efficiency and radiography](/asme/joint-efficiency).

## Heads are formed thin

Forming thins the plate, most at the knuckle. Order the head with a **minimum thickness after forming** equal to or above the required thickness plus corrosion; the head maker adds their own thinning allowance. The minimum thickness after forming goes on the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## Flat heads and covers

Flat heads, blind flanges and bolted covers are designed under UG-34 instead, with a factor for how the head is attached. They are far thicker than a formed head for the same pressure, which is why formed heads are used wherever they fit.

The finished vessel is proved by the [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test), at a pressure set from its [MAWP](/asme/mawp).

title: ASME hydrostatic test pressure calculator (UG-99)
question: What is the ASME hydrostatic test pressure for a pressure vessel?
answer: For a Section VIII Division 1 vessel, the minimum hydrostatic test pressure is 1.3 times the MAWP, multiplied by the lowest ratio of allowable stress at test temperature to allowable stress at design temperature (UG-99(b)). A pneumatic test uses 1.1 instead (UG-100). A Section I boiler is tested to at least 1.5 times its MAWP (PG-99).
description: ASME hydrostatic test pressure with a free calculator: UG-99 (1.3 × MAWP × stress ratio), pneumatic UG-100 (1.1), Section I PG-99 (1.5), procedure and gauges.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section I and Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## The rules

| Equipment | Test | Minimum test pressure |
|---|---|---|
| Section VIII Div. 1 vessel | Hydrostatic, UG-99(b) | 1.3 × MAWP × stress ratio |
| Section VIII Div. 1 vessel | Pneumatic, UG-100 | 1.1 × MAWP × stress ratio |
| Section I boiler | Hydrostatic, PG-99 | 1.5 × MAWP |

The **stress ratio** is the allowable stress at the test temperature divided by the allowable stress at the design temperature, taken for the material where that ratio is lowest. At ordinary temperatures the two are often equal and the ratio is 1, so the test is simply 1.3 × MAWP. For a hot vessel, whose allowable stress falls with temperature, the ratio is above 1 and the test pressure rises.

The test pressure is at the **top** of the vessel. If the gauge is at the bottom, add the static head of the water column.

## Example

A vessel with MAWP 100 psi at 650 °F, where the material's allowable stress is 20,000 psi at test temperature and 16,000 psi at 650 °F: 1.3 × 100 × (20,000 ÷ 16,000) = **162.5 psi**. In metric units it reads the same: MAWP 10 bar with the same materials gives 1.3 × 10 × 1.25 = **16.25 bar**. The calculator above does this for any rule and unit.

## How the test is done (Division 1)

- **Water temperature**: the metal should be at least 30 °F (17 °C) above the [MDMT](/asme/impact-testing) to avoid brittle fracture, and Division 1 recommends not above 120 °F (49 °C) so the vessel can be approached safely.
- **Inspection**: after reaching test pressure, it is reduced to at least the test pressure divided by 1.3 and held while every joint and connection is examined, normally with the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) present.
- **Gauges**: the dial should read about twice the test pressure, and never less than 1.5 or more than 4 times it (UG-102). Calibrate before the test.
- **Vents**: vent the high points so no air is trapped.

## Pneumatic tests

A gas stores far more energy than water at the same pressure, so a pneumatic test is used only where water can't be: vessels that can't be supported full, or that must not see any water. Division 1 adds conditions (examination of certain welds first, raising pressure in steps from half the test pressure), and the inspection pressure is the test pressure divided by 1.1.

## On the paperwork

The test pressure goes on the [data report](/asme/data-reports) and the nameplate record. How MAWP is set is in [MAWP and design pressure](/asme/mawp); the Indian practice for boilers is in [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: MDMT and impact test exemptions (UCS-66)
question: When is impact testing required for an ASME pressure vessel?
answer: Carbon and low-alloy steels can turn brittle when cold, so ASME Section VIII Division 1 requires Charpy impact tests unless an exemption applies. UCS-66 gives exemption curves (A to D) by material and thickness against the vessel's MDMT; thin parts and lower stresses earn more exemption. Below about −55 °F (−48 °C) most parts need testing.
description: ASME impact testing and MDMT explained: UCS-66 exemption curves A to D, governing thickness, the stress-ratio reduction, UG-20(f), and what testing involves.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## Why it matters

Steel that is tough at room temperature can fracture like glass when cold. The **MDMT** (minimum design metal temperature) is the coldest the metal may be while the vessel is at pressure; impact testing proves the steel, welds and heat-affected zones are tough at that temperature. See [MAWP and MDMT](/asme/mawp).

## How the exemption works

For carbon and low-alloy steels (Part UCS), Division 1 works it out part by part:

1. **Assign the material to a curve.** Figure UCS-66 has curves A to D. Curve A is for materials with the least toughness assurance; Curve D for the best (for example, normalized fine-grain plate). The curve assignments are listed in the Code.
2. **Find the governing thickness** of each part: for a butt joint, the thicker of the two members, with rules for other joints.
3. **Read the curve.** It gives the coldest MDMT allowed without impact testing at that thickness. If the vessel's MDMT is warmer, the part is exempt.
4. **Take credit for low stress.** When the part is less stressed than its full allowable (thicker than needed, or at lower pressure), Figure UCS-66.1 allows a further reduction in the exemption temperature.

There's also a blanket exemption for simple cases (UG-20(f)): P-No. 1 materials of limited thickness, hydrostatically tested to UG-99(b), with design temperatures between −20 °F (−29 °C) and 650 °F (343 °C) and no unusual shock or cyclic loading.

Below −55 °F (−48 °C), impact testing is generally required unless the part is very lightly stressed.

## What impact testing involves

Charpy V-notch specimens are cut from the material, or from a test weld for welds and heat-affected zones, and broken at the test temperature. The energy absorbed must meet a minimum that depends on the material's strength and thickness (UG-84). When impact testing applies, the welding procedure must also be qualified with impact tests, which brings in Section IX's supplementary [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

## Practical points

- Specify MDMT honestly: too warm is unsafe; too cold forces testing you didn't need.
- Buy plate to a specification and heat treatment on the better curves (normalized SA-516, for example) when the MDMT is cold.
- The MDMT and any impact test results go on the [data report](/asme/data-reports), and the steel's own test results come on its [MTR](/asme/mtr).

title: Joint efficiency and radiography (UW-11, UW-12)
question: What is joint efficiency in ASME Section VIII?
answer: Joint efficiency (E) is the factor ASME Section VIII Division 1 applies to a welded joint in the thickness formulas. It depends on the joint type and how much it is radiographed: a double-welded butt joint is 1.0 with full radiography, 0.85 with spot radiography and 0.70 with none (UW-12). Less radiography means a thicker shell.
description: ASME UW-12 joint efficiency values by joint type and radiography, joint categories A to D, when full radiography is mandatory (UW-11), and the cost trade-off.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## Joint efficiency by type and examination

Section VIII Division 1, Table UW-12, for the common butt joints:

| Joint type | Description | Full radiography | Spot radiography | None |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Double-welded butt joint, or equivalent full penetration | 1.00 | 0.85 | 0.70 |
| 2 | Single-welded butt joint with a backing strip left in | 0.90 | 0.80 | 0.65 |
| 3 | Single-welded butt joint without backing | – | – | 0.60 |

Lap and fillet joints have lower values again and are limited in where they may be used.

## Joint categories

Division 1 names joints by **location**, because location decides how much stress they carry:

- **Category A**: longitudinal welds in shells and nozzles, and the welds joining a hemispherical head to the shell. They carry the higher (hoop) stress.
- **Category B**: circumferential welds between shell courses and between shell and most formed heads.
- **Category C**: welds attaching flanges, tubesheets and flat heads.
- **Category D**: welds attaching nozzles and communicating chambers.

Type is what the joint is; category is where it is. Both go on the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## When full radiography is required

UW-11 makes full radiography of butt welds mandatory in several cases, among them:

- vessels in **lethal service**;
- butt welds thicker than a limit set by the material (for carbon steel, 1¼ in, 32 mm);
- **unfired steam boilers** above 50 psi (3.4 bar);
- where the designer has used E = 1.0.

Otherwise the designer chooses, and the choice is commercial: full radiography costs more in examination and saves steel by allowing E = 1.0.

## Seamless parts

A seamless shell or head has no longitudinal joint, but its efficiency still depends on the circumferential welds joining it: with those spot radiographed to the rule for this case, a seamless part uses E = 1.0; without, 0.85.

## Where it is used

E goes straight into the [shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) and [head](/asme/heads) formulas. The method and acceptance standards for the radiographs come from [Section V](/asme/section-v) and UW-51 (full) or UW-52 (spot).

title: MAWP, design pressure, operating pressure and MDMT
question: What is the difference between MAWP and design pressure?
answer: Design pressure is the pressure the vessel is designed for, set from the process with a margin. MAWP is the highest pressure the finished vessel can take at the top, at its design temperature, worked out from the thicknesses actually used; it is at least the design pressure. Operating pressure sits below both, and the relief valve is set at or below MAWP.
description: MAWP vs design pressure vs operating pressure in ASME Section VIII, how they relate to the relief valve set pressure, and what MDMT means on a nameplate.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## Four pressures, in order

| Pressure | What it is | Who sets it |
|---|---|---|
| Operating pressure | What the process normally runs at | The process |
| Relief set pressure | Where the relief device opens; at or below MAWP | The designer, within Code limits |
| Design pressure | What the vessel is designed for, at the top, with the coincident temperature | The owner or designer (UG-21) |
| MAWP | The most the completed vessel can take at the top, at the design temperature, from its actual thicknesses | Calculated (UG-98) |

A common margin is design pressure about 10% above the maximum operating pressure, or 25 psi (1.7 bar) above it for low pressures, so normal swings don't lift the relief valve. That margin is practice, not a Code rule.

## Why MAWP can be higher than design pressure

Plates come in standard thicknesses. If the [shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) needed for the design pressure is 0.30 in (7.6 mm) and you use 0.375 in (9.5 mm) plate, the shell can take more. MAWP is worked out back from each part's thickness, less corrosion allowance, and the weakest part sets it. Many owners simply set MAWP equal to design pressure to keep the relief valve and nameplate simple; that's allowed.

MAWP is stated at the **top** of the vessel in its operating position. Parts lower down see the static head of the liquid too, and are designed for it.

## Hot and corroded, new and cold

The thickness used for MAWP is the **corroded** thickness at the **design temperature**. Some owners also ask for MAP (maximum allowable pressure, new and cold), which is higher. The [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) is set from MAWP.

## MDMT

The **minimum design metal temperature** is the coldest metal temperature the vessel may see at its MAWP: a cold winter start-up, an autorefrigerating flash, a cold fluid. It decides whether materials need impact testing; see [MDMT and impact testing](/asme/impact-testing). Both MAWP at its temperature and MDMT go on the nameplate and the [data report](/asme/data-reports).

## Overpressure

While a relief device is discharging, pressure may rise above MAWP by a set amount: in Division 1, generally 10% or 3 psi (0.2 bar) for a single device, 16% with several, 21% for fire exposure. See [Section XIII](/asme/section-xiii).

title: Material test reports (MTR) and heat number traceability
question: What does an MTR need to show for ASME pressure vessel material?
answer: A material test report (MTR, or mill test certificate) certifies one heat of material: its specification and grade, heat number, chemical analysis, mechanical test results and heat treatment. For ASME work the plate's heat number must match its MTR, stay legible or be transferred when the plate is cut (UG-77), and be recorded against every part.
description: ASME material traceability: what an MTR must show, heat numbers, UG-77 marking transfer, SA vs A on certificates, EN 10204 3.1, and records an Inspector checks.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)
Indian Boiler Regulations, 2026 (Gazette of India, Extraordinary, No. 596)
sources.publisher: Central Boilers Board, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade

checks.quote: A certificate in Form-V(Part-A) from the steel maker and a certificate from the maker of the plates or bars

body:
## What an MTR is

A mill makes steel in **heats** (one melt). The MTR certifies a heat, or a lot from it, against a specification:

| On the MTR | Why the shop checks it |
|---|---|
| Specification and grade, e.g. SA-516 Grade 70 ([common ones](/asme/items)) | Must match the drawing and the Code's accepted specification; see [Section II](/asme/section-ii) for SA vs A |
| Heat number (and slab or plate number) | The link between the paper and the steel |
| Chemical analysis | Within the specification's limits |
| Tensile and yield strength, elongation | Within the specification |
| Heat treatment (as-rolled, normalized) | Affects the impact test curve; see [impact testing](/asme/impact-testing) |
| Charpy results, if ordered | Needed when the part isn't exempt from impact testing |
| Supplementary requirements | E.g. ultrasonic examination, simulated PWHT |
| Certification statement and signature | The mill's certification |

India and Europe usually call it a [material test certificate](/systems/material-test-certificate) and order it to EN 10204 type 3.1; the US says MTR or CMTR. The content the Code needs is the same.

## The Code's rules, in outline

- **Receiving** (UG-93): plate for pressure parts comes with the mill's certified test report; the shop checks it against the material and keeps it. Other product forms (pipe, forgings, fittings) need the certification the Code allows for that form.
- **Marking** (UG-94 and the material specification): the material carries its specification, grade and heat number.
- **Cutting** (UG-77): when plate is cut, the marking is transferred to every piece that goes into the vessel before it's cut, or a coded system is used that the Inspector accepts, so each piece stays traceable.
- **Records**: the quality control manual describes how; see [the quality control manual](/asme/quality-control-manual).

## Where traceability breaks

- Offcuts and remnants returned to stock without their heat number, then reused on the next job.
- One MTR filed for a delivery that held two heats.
- Nozzle necks and pipe cut from a length whose marking ended up on the scrap end.
- MTRs scanned into a folder with no link to the parts they cover.

Each of these turns up at the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector)'s check of the [data report](/asme/data-reports) package. A system that keeps [material traceability](/systems/material-traceability), recording the heat number at receipt and carries it to every cut piece, remnant and weld removes the search at the end.

## In India

IBR 2026 asks for the steel maker's certificate in Form V Part A and an extract of every material certificate (Form V Part B) with the registration papers, and lists ASME SA specifications among acceptable materials. See [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr) and [IBR Form V Part A](/ibr/forms/form-v-part-a).

title: National Board registration, the NB mark and the R stamp
question: What is National Board registration for a pressure vessel?
answer: National Board registration files a stamped boiler's or vessel's data report with the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors, which keeps it permanently; the item then carries the NB mark. Most US jurisdictions require it for installation. The National Board also runs the R stamp program for repairs and alterations under its inspection code, the NBIC.
description: National Board registration and the NB mark, the NBIC, and the R, VR, NR and T/O stamps for repairs, relief valves and testing, explained for shops and owners.

sources.title: Registration
sources.publisher: The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors

sources.title: Accreditation programs for repairs, alterations and relief valve testing (R, VR, NR, T/O)
sources.publisher: The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors

sources.title: Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certificates of Authorization and the Certification Mark: Informational Handbook (BPV-GUI-03)

checks.quote: registration of data report forms may be required by the legal authority of a state or municipality of the United States or province of Canada.

body:
## Who the National Board is

The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors is made up of the chief boiler inspectors of US states and Canadian provinces. ASME writes the construction code; the National Board commissions inspectors, keeps the registry of built items, and writes the code for equipment once it's in service, the **National Board Inspection Code (NBIC)**.

## Registration and the NB mark

Registration is the last step after design and construction and inspection: the manufacturer sends the signed [data report](/asme/data-reports) to the National Board, which keeps it on permanent record, and the nameplate carries the **NB** mark with a National Board number.

- A manufacturer becomes **authorized to register** by meeting the National Board's criteria (its document NB-264). Authorization is free; each registered item has a fee.
- Reports are filed on paper or electronically, within 30 days of certification, on current forms.
- Registration is required by most US jurisdictions for pressure equipment to be installed. Check the jurisdiction for the place of installation; see [US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

For an owner, registration means a lost data report can always be replaced, which matters at every later inspection, repair or sale.

## The NBIC

The NBIC has four parts: installation, inspection, repairs and alterations, and pressure relief devices. It is the rulebook for the equipment's life after the ASME stamp.

## R, VR, NR and T/O

| Stamp | For |
|---|---|
| R | Repairs and alterations to boilers and pressure vessels |
| VR | Repair of pressure relief valves |
| NR | Repairs and replacements of nuclear components |
| T/O | Testing of pressure relief valves |

A company gets one by having its quality system manual evaluated and showing it works, much like an ASME [joint review](/asme/u-stamp). R-stamp work is accepted by a National Board commissioned inspector, and the holder keeps an agreement with an inspection agency. Repairs are recorded on NBIC forms (R-1 for a repair, R-2 for an alteration) and, for registered items, filed with the National Board too.

title: P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers in ASME Section IX
question: What is a P-number in welding?
answer: A P-number groups base metals with similar welding behaviour, so a procedure or welder test on one covers the others in the group: P-No. 1 is carbon steel, P-No. 8 austenitic stainless. F-numbers group filler metals by usability, such as F-4 for low-hydrogen electrodes like E7018, and A-numbers group steel weld metal by chemistry.
description: ASME Section IX P-numbers, Group numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers explained, with common materials and electrodes in each.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section IX: Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications)

body:
## Why groups exist

There are thousands of material specifications. Without grouping, every pairing would need its own procedure test. Section IX assigns each base metal a **P-number** (and, for ferrous metals where toughness matters, a **Group number**), so a PQR on one material qualifies the others in its P-number. The full assignments are in Section IX (QW/QB-422) and Section II Part D; the common ones are below.

## Common P-numbers

| P-No. | Materials | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Carbon and carbon-manganese steels | SA-516 Gr 70, SA-106 Gr B, SA-105 |
| 3 | C–½Mo and low-chromium steels | SA-204, SA-335 P1 |
| 4 | 1–1¼Cr–½Mo steels | SA-387 Gr 11, SA-335 P11 |
| 5A | 2¼Cr–1Mo steels | SA-387 Gr 22, SA-335 P22 |
| 5B | 5Cr to 9Cr steels | SA-335 P5, P9 |
| 7 | Ferritic stainless | SA-240 Type 405, 409, 430 |
| 8 | Austenitic stainless | SA-240 Type 304, 316, 321 |
| 10H | Duplex stainless | SA-240 S31803, S32205 |
| 15E | Creep-strength enhanced ferritic steels | SA-335 P91 |
| 21–26 | Aluminum alloys | SB-209 5083 |
| 31–35 | Copper alloys | SB-171 |
| 41–49 | Nickel alloys | SB-168 Alloy 600, SB-443 Alloy 625 |
| 51–53 | Titanium | SB-265 Grade 2 |

Welding a P-No. 1 to a P-No. 8 is a dissimilar-metal joint and needs a procedure qualified for that combination.

The [materials list](/asme/items) gives the P-number of each common boiler and vessel material.

## F-numbers: filler metal usability

| F-No. | Filler | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Heavy iron-powder steel electrodes | E7024 |
| 2 | Rutile steel electrodes | E6013 |
| 3 | Cellulosic steel electrodes | E6010, E6011 |
| 4 | Low-hydrogen steel electrodes | E7018 |
| 5 | Stainless steel electrodes | E308L-16 |
| 6 | Solid and metal-cored steel wires and rods (GTAW, GMAW, SAW) | ER70S-6 |
| 43 | Nickel alloy filler | ERNiCrMo-3 |

F-numbers matter most for **welders**: they reflect how hard the electrode is to handle, so a welder qualified with F-4 is generally also qualified for F-1 to F-3 in the same process, but not the other way round. Section IX's QW-433 table has the exact pairings, including the effect of welding with or without backing.

## A-numbers: weld metal chemistry

A-numbers classify the deposited weld metal of steels by composition (A-1 carbon steel, A-2 carbon–molybdenum, up to A-8 austenitic chromium–nickel and others). A change of A-number is a procedure [essential variable](/asme/essential-variables) for most processes.

## Using them well

- Write the P-number, Group number, F-number and A-number on every WPS and PQR; reviewers check them first.
- Check the material's P-number in the current edition: new materials are added and occasionally regrouped.
- The base metal's specification and grade come from its [MTR](/asme/mtr); see [Section II](/asme/section-ii) for SA vs A.

The documents these numbers appear on are explained in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq).

title: Post-weld heat treatment requirements (UCS-56)
question: When is post-weld heat treatment required by ASME?
answer: ASME Section VIII Division 1 requires post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) by material and thickness: Table UCS-56 sets, for each P-number, the holding temperature, the time per inch of thickness and when it can be skipped. For P-No. 1 carbon steel, PWHT is generally required above 1½ in (38 mm), held at 1,100 °F (595 °C) or more, and some services need it at any thickness.
description: ASME PWHT requirements under UCS-56: holding temperature and time for P-No. 1, thickness exemptions, service-driven PWHT, heating and cooling rates and records.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## Why heat treat after welding

Welding leaves high residual stresses and hard zones next to the weld. PWHT (stress relieving) heats the part below its transformation temperature and holds it, which relaxes the stresses and tempers the hard zones. It improves toughness and resistance to some kinds of cracking, at the cost of furnace time and, sometimes, strength.

## The table, for P-No. 1 carbon steel

Table UCS-56-1 sets requirements by P-number. For P-No. 1 (carbon steel, the commonest case), in outline:

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Minimum holding temperature | 1,100 °F (595 °C) |
| Holding time, up to 2 in (50 mm) thick | 1 hour per inch, at least 15 minutes |
| Holding time, over 2 in (50 mm) | Longer, on a sliding scale in the table |
| Exemption by thickness | PWHT is not mandatory up to 1¼ in (32 mm), and up to 1½ in (38 mm) with a minimum preheat, subject to the table's notes |

Other P-numbers have their own temperatures and much narrower exemptions; chromium–molybdenum steels (P-No. 4, 5A) nearly always need it. Check the current edition's table for your material: the notes carry most of the detail.

## When service decides, not thickness

PWHT can be required whatever the thickness:

- **Lethal service** (UW-2): Division 1 requires PWHT of carbon and low-alloy steel vessels.
- **Low temperature**: some impact test exemptions depend on it; see [impact testing](/asme/impact-testing).
- **The owner's specification**: caustic, amine, wet H₂S and similar services often call for PWHT to resist stress-corrosion cracking, beyond the Code's minimum.

## Doing it

- Heating and cooling rates above 800 °F (425 °C) are limited by thickness (UCS-56(d)), so a thick vessel takes a long cycle.
- Temperatures are recorded by thermocouples on the part, and the chart is part of the record.
- PWHT is a procedure [essential variable](/asme/essential-variables): adding or removing it needs a PQR qualified that way.

## On the paperwork

The PWHT chart goes in the [data report](/asme/data-reports) package and PWHT is declared on the report itself. In India, IBR asks for heat treatment charts of welded drums with the registration documents; see [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: The ASME quality control manual: what it must cover
question: What should an ASME quality control manual include?
answer: An ASME quality control manual describes, in English, how the shop meets every Code requirement in its scope: who has authority, how drawings and calculations are controlled, how material is received and traced, welding, NDE, heat treatment, calibration, nonconformities, inspection and records. The joint review checks the manual, then checks the shop works the way it says.
description: What an ASME quality control manual must cover for a U or S certificate: the elements Section VIII lists and how the joint review tests it.

sources.title: Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certificates of Authorization and the Certification Mark: Informational Handbook (BPV-GUI-03)

checks.quote: While the Applicant must address each element of the QCS in the Code, the Applicant need only demonstrate those elements within the intended scope of activities that apply to their program.
The Manual need not follow the format of this Guide.

body:
## What it is for

The manual is the written description of the shop's quality control system. ASME doesn't certify a product; it certifies that the shop has a system that will keep producing Code items, and the manual is how that system is described. At the [joint review](/asme/u-stamp) the team reads the manual, then watches the shop do what it says.

## The elements

For Section VIII Division 1 the elements are listed in its quality control system appendix (Mandatory Appendix 10 in recent editions); Section I and the others have equivalents. In outline:

| Element | What the manual says |
|---|---|
| Authority and responsibility | Who is responsible for quality, and that they can stop work |
| Organization | An org chart showing the quality function's independence |
| Drawings, calculations and specifications | How they are prepared or received, checked, approved, revised and issued |
| Material control | Receiving, checking against the [MTR](/asme/mtr), marking and [traceability](/asme/mtr) through cutting |
| Examination and inspection program | What is checked, when, and the Inspector's hold points |
| Correction of nonconformities | How a nonconformity is recorded, decided and closed |
| Welding | [WPS, PQR and WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq) control, welder identification, [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity) |
| Nondestructive examination | Procedures to [Section V](/asme/section-v), personnel qualification |
| Heat treatment | Procedures and records, including [PWHT](/asme/pwht) charts |
| Calibration | Gauges and test equipment, intervals and records |
| Records retention | Which records are kept, where, for how long |
| Sample forms | Every form the manual refers to |
| Inspection of vessels and parts | How the Authorized Inspector is given access and information |
| Relief valves | How they are inspected, where in scope |

ASME also gives applicants a checklist to cross-reference each element to the manual's paragraphs; the completed checklist goes to the review team.

## What makes a manual pass

- **It describes this shop.** A bought template with another company's job titles and forms fails the moment the team asks someone to show a step.
- **Every form exists and is used.** The forms in the manual are the forms on the shop floor.
- **Records join up.** A reviewer picks a weld on the demonstration item and follows it to the welder, their qualification, the WPS, the PQR, the filler metal and the NDE report. Each link has to be there.

That last test is the one most shops find hardest on paper and easiest in software: a record per weld, heat number and welder, linked once, rather than files cross-referenced by hand.

title: ASME Section I vs IV: power vs heating boilers
question: What is the difference between ASME Section I and Section IV boilers?
answer: Section IV covers heating boilers: steam boilers up to 15 psi (1 bar), and hot water boilers up to 160 psi (11 bar) and 250 °F (121 °C). Anything above those limits is a power boiler under Section I, which has stricter design, material, examination and inspection rules. The stamps differ too: S for Section I power boilers, H for Section IV heating boilers.
description: ASME Section I power boilers vs Section IV heating boilers: the pressure and temperature limits, stamps, data reports and what changes for the shop.

sources.title: Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certification (designators S, A, E, M, PP, H, HLW)
ASME Data Report Forms

body:
## Where the line is

| | Section IV (heating boilers) | Section I (power boilers) |
|---|---|---|
| Steam boilers | Up to 15 psi (1 bar) | Above 15 psi (1 bar) |
| Hot water boilers | Up to 160 psi (11 bar) and 250 °F (121 °C) | Above 160 psi (11 bar) or above 250 °F (121 °C) |
| Typical use | Space heating, domestic hot water | Process steam, power generation, high-temperature hot water |
| Certification designator | H (HLW for lined potable water heaters) | S, with A for assembly, E for electric, M for miniature, PP for boiler piping |
| Main data reports | H-2, H-3 (H-5 and H-5A for cast iron and cast aluminum) | P-2, P-3, P-4 |

Section IV allows cast iron and cast aluminum sectional boilers, which Section I does not, and its rules are simpler throughout because the energy stored at low pressure is much smaller.

## What changes for the shop

- **Design**: Section I has its own formulas (Part PG) and sets thicknesses for drums, headers and tubes in the hot zone; Section IV's are simpler and include minimum thicknesses.
- **Examination**: more volumetric examination of welds in Section I.
- **Testing**: a Section I boiler is hydrostatically tested to at least 1.5 times its maximum allowable working pressure (PG-99); the [hydrostatic test guide](/asme/hydrostatic-test) has a calculator.
- **Piping**: boiler external piping, from the boiler to the first stop valve and beyond as the Code defines it, is part of the Section I boiler and is built to [B31.1](/asme/b31-1-vs-b31-3) by a holder of a Section I certificate that covers it (S, A or PP).
- **Inspection**: both need an [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector), except Section IV cast iron and cast aluminum boilers, whose certificate needs no inspection agency agreement (see [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps)).

## In India

Boilers in India are registered under the Indian Boiler Regulations, 2026, whichever ASME section they were designed to. How the two fit together is in [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: ASME Section II materials and SA vs A specifications
question: What is the difference between SA-516 and A516?
answer: ASME Section II holds the material specifications the Code allows: Part A ferrous, Part B nonferrous, Part C filler metals, Part D properties and allowable stresses. An SA specification is ASME's adoption of an ASTM one, sometimes with changes; SA-516 is ASME's version of ASTM A516. Code pressure parts must be certified to the SA specification, often on a dual-marked MTR.
description: ASME Section II explained: Parts A, B, C and D, SA vs A (SA-516 vs A516), dual certification, and where the allowable stress values come from.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section II, Parts A to D)

body:
## The four Parts

| Part | Contents | Typical specifications |
|---|---|---|
| A | Ferrous material specifications | SA-516 plate, SA-106 pipe, SA-105 forgings, SA-240 stainless plate |
| B | Nonferrous material specifications | SB-168 nickel alloy plate, SB-209 aluminum plate |
| C | Welding rods, electrodes and filler metals | SFA-5.1 (carbon steel electrodes such as E7018), SFA-5.18 (GMAW and GTAW wires) |
| D | Properties | Allowable stresses, tensile and yield strength at temperature, external pressure charts, physical properties |

Part D comes in customary (psi, °F) and metric volumes. The [shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness) and [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) calculators both need its allowable stress values, which is why those tools ask you for them rather than supply them: the tables are ASME's, and they change between editions.

The specifications a boiler or vessel shop buys most, with P-numbers and their IBR 2026 status, are in the [materials list](/asme/items).

## SA vs A

ASTM writes most of the material standards; ASME adopts them into Section II, adds an "S" (SA, SB) and sometimes adds requirements. Section II prints each adopted specification with a note of which ASTM edition it matches and any differences.

What that means in practice:

- A pressure part must be certified to the SA specification (or to an ASTM edition the Code accepts as identical), not just "A516".
- Mills therefore often **dual-certify**: the MTR reads "SA-516/A516 Grade 70", stating it meets both.
- If an MTR shows only the ASTM number, the [MTR guide](/asme/mtr) explains what the Code lets you do about it, and the Inspector decides whether it is acceptable.

## Allowable stress in Part D

Section VIII Division 1 and Section I take their maximum allowable stresses from Part D tables (Table 1A for ferrous materials, Table 1B for nonferrous), by specification, grade and temperature. Division 2 has its own, higher, values because of its smaller design margin; see [Section VIII Division 1 vs 2](/asme/section-viii).

## Welding consumables

Part C's SFA specifications classify filler metals; Section IX then groups them by F-number and A-number for qualification. See [P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers](/asme/p-numbers). In India, IBR 2026 classifies covered electrodes by these same SFA specifications or AWS ones; see [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: ASME Section IX: welding, brazing and fusing qualifications
question: What is ASME Section IX?
answer: ASME Section IX sets how a shop qualifies its welding procedures and its welders. A procedure is qualified by welding a test coupon and testing it (the PQR), then written up as a WPS; each welder is qualified by a test of their own (the WPQ). Section IX doesn't decide where welds go or how they're examined: the construction section does.
description: ASME Section IX explained: what it covers, its parts (QG, QW, QB, QF), WPS, PQR and WPQ, and how it works with Sections I and VIII and the B31 piping codes.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section IX: Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications)
Summary of Changes to ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section IX (Welding Journal, July 2025)

body:
## What Section IX does, and what it doesn't

Section IX answers two questions: **can this procedure make a sound weld**, and **can this person make it**. It does that with test coupons and mechanical or volumetric tests, and with rules for how far a passed test stretches (which materials, thicknesses, positions and processes it covers).

It does not say which joints need welding, what type of joint, which welds are radiographed or when heat treatment is needed. That is the construction section's job: [Section VIII](/asme/section-viii), Section I, or a B31 piping code, which then sends you to Section IX for qualification.

## Its parts

| Part | Covers |
|---|---|
| QG | General requirements shared by all processes |
| QW | Welding: procedure qualification (QW-200), performance qualification (QW-300), the variables (QW-400) and standard welding procedure specifications (QW-500) |
| QB | Brazing |
| QF | Plastic fusing (polyethylene pipe) |

## The three documents

- **WPS** (welding procedure specification): the written instructions a welder follows, with ranges for each variable.
- **PQR** (procedure qualification record): the record of the test coupon that proves the WPS works: what was actually used, and the test results.
- **WPQ** (welder or welding operator performance qualification): the record that a person passed their test, and what it qualifies them for.

How the three link, and what goes in each, is in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq). Which changes need a new PQR is in [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables); which positions a welder's test covers is in [welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification); and how a welder keeps their qualification alive is the [continuity rule](/asme/welder-continuity).

## Material grouping

Section IX groups base metals by **P-number** and filler metals by **F-number** and **A-number**, so one test covers a family of materials instead of one specification. See [P-numbers, F-numbers and A-numbers](/asme/p-numbers).

## The 2025 Edition

The Section IX changes in the 2025 Edition became mandatory for new qualifications on 1 January 2026, as the Welding Journal's summary of changes notes. Existing qualifications made to earlier editions stay valid; the [editions guide](/asme/editions) explains how that works.

title: ASME Section V: nondestructive examination
question: What is ASME Section V?
answer: ASME Section V sets how nondestructive examinations are done: radiography, ultrasonic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, visual and leak testing, each in its own Article. It covers the method, not the verdict: which welds are examined and what counts as a rejectable flaw come from the construction section, such as Section VIII or Section I.
description: ASME Section V explained: its Articles for RT, UT, MT, PT, VT and leak testing, who sets acceptance criteria, and how NDE personnel are qualified.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section V: Nondestructive Examination)

body:
## Method in Section V, verdict in the construction section

A radiograph is taken the way Section V says: film or digital, source and geometry, image quality indicators, density. Whether the indication on it is acceptable is judged by the construction section: in Section VIII Division 1, for example, full radiography is judged under UW-51 and spot radiography under UW-52. That split is why an NDE procedure cites Section V and the report cites Section VIII.

## The main Articles

| Article | Method |
|---|---|
| 1 | General requirements |
| 2 | Radiographic examination (RT), film and digital |
| 4 | Ultrasonic examination (UT) of welds, including phased array and TOFD |
| 6 | Liquid penetrant examination (PT) |
| 7 | Magnetic particle examination (MT) |
| 9 | Visual examination (VT) |
| 10 | Leak testing |
| 23 | Material specifications for NDE (adopted ASTM standards) |

## Personnel

The construction sections require NDE personnel to be qualified and certified to a written practice. In US and Canadian shops that is usually the employer's written practice to ASNT's SNT-TC-1A, with Level I, II and III personnel. IBR 2026 accepts ASNT certificates alongside the Indian Society for Non-destructive Testing's; see [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

## Where it meets the rest of the Code

- How much radiography a joint gets changes its **joint efficiency** and so its required thickness: see [joint efficiency and radiography](/asme/joint-efficiency).
- NDE reports go into the vessel's file and are listed on the [data report](/asme/data-reports) package.
- A welder can be qualified by radiography instead of bend tests for most processes; see [welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification).

title: ASME Section VIII: Division 1 vs 2 vs 3
question: What is the difference between ASME Section VIII Division 1 and Division 2?
answer: Section VIII sets the rules for pressure vessels. Division 1 is design by rule with a larger safety margin and is used for most vessels. Division 2 allows thinner walls in return for more design analysis, stricter material and examination rules, and a certified design report. Division 3 is for very high pressures, usually above 10,000 psi (690 bar).
description: ASME Section VIII Division 1, 2 and 3 compared: design margin, analysis, examination, paperwork and stamps, and how to choose for a pressure vessel.

sources.title: Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certification (certification designators U, UM, U2, U3)
ASME Data Report Forms

body:
## What Section VIII covers

Section VIII is the Code's pressure vessel section: tanks, columns, reactors, heat exchangers, receivers and similar vessels that hold internal or external pressure. Division 1 itself excludes some equipment, for example vessels designed for 15 psi (1 bar) or less, and very small vessels (6 in, 152 mm, inside diameter or less), which is why many low-pressure tanks are built to other standards. Fired equipment that generates steam belongs to [Section I](/asme/section-i-vs-iv).

## The three Divisions side by side

| | Division 1 | Division 2 | Division 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approach | Design by rule: formulas and charts | Design by rule or by analysis (stress analysis, finite elements) | Design by analysis, fracture mechanics |
| Typical use | Most vessels | Large, thick or high-pressure vessels where thinner walls save money | Very high pressure, usually above 10,000 psi (690 bar) |
| Design margin on tensile strength | 3.5 | 2.4 | Based on yield, with further checks |
| Owner's input | Design conditions on the order | A User's Design Specification | A User's Design Specification |
| Design certification | The manufacturer | A Manufacturer's Design Report, certified as the Division requires | As Division 2, plus more |
| Certification designator | U (UM for miniature vessels) | U2 | U3 |
| Data report | U-1 or U-1A | A-1 | K-1 |

The smaller margin is the reason Division 2 exists: the same vessel needs less steel. The price is engineering. Division 2 demands more analysis, more examination of welds and materials, and documents that Division 1 doesn't, so it pays off mainly on large, thick or alloy vessels where steel is the bigger cost.

## How to choose

- **Start with Division 1** unless there's a reason not to. More shops hold a U certificate, more inspectors know it, and the paperwork is lighter.
- **Consider Division 2** when the wall gets thick (a rough sign: shells over about 2 in, 50 mm), the material is expensive, or the vessel is cyclic and needs a fatigue assessment anyway.
- **Division 3** is a specialist field (isostatic presses, high-pressure reactors).

A shop can only stamp what its certificate covers: a U certificate does not allow Division 2 work. See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).

## What a Division 1 vessel's paperwork looks like

The design calculations ([shell thickness](/asme/shell-thickness), [heads](/asme/heads), nozzles, flanges), material certificates ([MTRs](/asme/mtr)), welding procedures and welder qualifications ([WPS, PQR and WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq)), examination reports, the [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) record, and finally the [Manufacturer's Data Report](/asme/data-reports), signed by the manufacturer and the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector). ASME's 2025 forms list for Division 1 also includes User's Design Requirements forms (U-DR-1 and U-DR-2) for the owner's design conditions.

title: ASME Section XIII: relief valves and overpressure protection
question: What is ASME Section XIII?
answer: Section XIII, first published in the 2021 Edition, holds the Code's rules for pressure relief devices: relief valves, rupture disks and pin devices, how their capacity is certified and how they are marked. The construction sections still say when a boiler or vessel needs protection; Section XIII says what the device must be.
description: ASME Section XIII explained: why relief device rules moved there in 2021, the UV, V, HV and UD stamps, capacity certification and what stayed in Section VIII.

sources.title: 2021 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (new Section XIII: Rules for Overpressure Protection)
Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certification (Section XIII designators)
Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certificates of Authorization and the Certification Mark: Informational Handbook (BPV-GUI-03)

checks.quote: it is necessary that all required capacity certification tests be scheduled within ninety days from the date of the review. If the tests are not successfully completed within six months from the date of the review, a new review must be conducted.

body:
## Why it exists

Until 2021 each construction section carried its own relief device rules: Section VIII Division 1 in its UG-125 series of paragraphs, Section IV and Section I in theirs. The 2021 Edition gathered the device rules into one new section so that a valve maker works to one book. The construction sections kept the requirement to protect the equipment and point to Section XIII for the device. In older drawings and data sheets you'll still see "UG-125"; on new work the device side is Section XIII.

## The device stamps

| Designator | Device |
|---|---|
| V | Boiler pressure relief valves |
| HV | Heating boiler safety valves |
| UV | Pressure vessel pressure relief valves |
| UD | Pressure vessel nonreclosing devices (rupture disks and similar) |
| UV3, UD3 | High-pressure vessel devices (Division 3) |
| TV, TD | Transport tank devices |

Unlike a vessel certificate, these need no agreement with an inspection agency. Instead, the National Board appoints the reviewer, and the device's relieving capacity has to be certified by test at an accepted laboratory; the time limits for those tests are quoted below. See [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps) for the full list.

## What stays with the vessel designer

The construction section still decides:

- that the vessel or boiler needs protection, and from what (a blocked outlet, a fire, a failed control);
- the set pressure, normally not above the [MAWP](/asme/mawp);
- how far pressure may rise while the device relieves: in Division 1, generally 10% or 3 psi (0.2 bar) above MAWP for one device, 16% with several, 21% for fire.

## Repairs

Setting and repairing relief valves in service is not ASME Section XIII work. It is done under the National Board's VR program; see [National Board registration and the R stamp](/asme/national-board-registration).

title: Shell thickness and MAWP (UG-27), with a calculator
question: How do you calculate pressure vessel shell thickness to ASME?
answer: For a cylindrical shell under internal pressure, ASME Section VIII Division 1 (UG-27) gives the required thickness as t = PR / (SE − 0.6P), where P is design pressure, R the inside radius, S the allowable stress and E the joint efficiency. Add the corrosion allowance, check the longitudinal-stress formula too, and take the larger.
description: ASME UG-27 shell thickness for cylinders and spheres, with a free calculator: formulas, corrosion allowance, joint efficiency and MAWP.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section VIII, Division 1)

body:
## The formulas

Section VIII Division 1, UG-27, for internal pressure, using the **inside radius in the corroded condition**:

| Shell | Required thickness | Valid while |
|---|---|---|
| Cylinder, circumferential stress (governs the longitudinal joints) | t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) | P ≤ 0.385SE and t ≤ R/2 |
| Cylinder, longitudinal stress (governs the circumferential joints) | t = PR / (2SE + 0.4P) | P ≤ 1.25SE and t ≤ R/2 |
| Sphere | t = PR / (2SE − 0.2P) | P ≤ 0.665SE and t ≤ 0.356R |

- **P**: design pressure, plus any static head at that point.
- **R**: inside radius, increased by the corrosion allowance.
- **S**: maximum allowable stress at the design temperature, from [Section II Part D](/asme/section-ii).
- **E**: [joint efficiency](/asme/joint-efficiency) of the relevant joint.

Outside the limits, use the thick-shell formulas in Mandatory Appendix 1-2. Each formula can also be rearranged to give the **MAWP** a known thickness allows; for a cylinder, P = SEt / (R + 0.6t).

## A worked example

A carbon steel shell, 48 in inside diameter, design pressure 150 psi, allowable stress 20,000 psi, spot radiographed Type 1 joints (E = 0.85), corrosion allowance 0.125 in:

1. Corroded radius: 24 + 0.125 = 24.125 in.
2. Circumferential: t = 150 × 24.125 / (20,000 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 150) = 3,618.75 / 16,910 = **0.214 in**.
3. Longitudinal: t = 150 × 24.125 / (2 × 20,000 × 0.85 + 0.4 × 150) = 0.106 in. Circumferential governs.
4. Add corrosion: 0.214 + 0.125 = **0.339 in** minimum.
5. Choose plate: ⅜ in (0.375) covers it, after allowing for any mill undertolerance and forming thin-out.

The same shell in metric: 1,220 mm inside diameter, design pressure 1.03 MPa (10.3 bar), allowable stress 138 MPa, E = 0.85, corrosion allowance 3 mm. Corroded radius 613 mm; t = 1.03 × 613 / (138 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 1.03) = **5.4 mm**, plus 3 mm corrosion = **8.4 mm**, so a 10 mm plate. Use MPa with mm, or psi with inches, and never mix them.

The calculator above repeats these steps for your numbers and works the MAWP back from a chosen thickness. The allowable stress is yours to enter: it comes from ASME's tables for your material, grade and temperature, which change between editions and aren't reproduced here.

## What the formula doesn't cover

- **Heads**: their own formulas; see [heads](/asme/heads).
- **Openings**: every nozzle needs reinforcement checked (UG-37 and onwards).
- **External pressure and vacuum**: a separate check (UG-28) with charts from Section II Part D; often thicker than internal pressure needs.
- **Other loads**: wind, seismic, supports, lifting and piping loads (UG-22).
- **Minimum thickness**: Division 1 sets a floor for shells and heads regardless of pressure (UG-16).

Related: [MAWP and design pressure](/asme/mawp), and the [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) that proves the result.

title: ASME stamps list: U, U2, S, H, PP, UV and R explained
question: What do the ASME U, S and R stamps mean?
answer: An ASME stamp is the ASME Certification Mark with a designator showing what the item is built to: U for a Section VIII Division 1 pressure vessel, U2 for Division 2, S for a Section I power boiler, H for a heating boiler, UV for a relief valve. Only a holder of that certificate may apply it. The R stamp is the National Board's, for repairs.

body:
## One mark, many designators

Since the early 2010s there has been one **ASME Certification Mark** (the cloverleaf), stamped together with a **designator**: the letters that say which section and which kind of work the item was built to. People still say "U stamp" for the mark with the U designator, and this guide does too.

## ASME designators

ASME's certification page lists these, with how long each certificate lasts and whether it needs an agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency (from ASME's informational handbook):

| Section | Designator | For | Valid | Inspection agency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | S | Power boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | A | Assembly of power boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | E | Electric boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | M | Miniature boilers | 3 years | Yes |
| I | PP | Pressure piping (boiler external piping) | 3 years | Yes |
| IV | H | Heating boilers (not cast iron or aluminum) | 3 years | Yes |
| IV | H | Cast iron and cast aluminum heating boilers | 1 year | No |
| IV | HLW | Lined potable water heaters | 3 years | Yes |
| VIII-1 | U | Pressure vessels | 3 years | Yes |
| VIII-1 | UM | Miniature pressure vessels (needs a U or S too) | 1 year | Through the U or S |
| VIII-2 | U2 | Pressure vessels, alternative rules | 3 years | Yes |
| VIII-3 | U3 | High-pressure vessels | 3 years | Yes |
| X | RP | Fiber-reinforced plastic vessels | 3 years | Yes |
| XII | T | Transport tanks | 3 years | Yes |
| I, IV, VIII-1, VIII-2, XII | PRT | Parts, without design responsibility | 3 years | Yes |
| XIII | V, HV, UV, UD, UV3, UD3, TV, TD | Relief valves and devices | 3 years | No |

PRT is for parts makers who build to someone else's design: the certificate holder who buys the part takes design responsibility. Relief device certificates have their own review route; see [Section XIII](/asme/section-xiii).

## National Board marks

These are not ASME's; they come from the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors:

- **NB**: the item's data report is registered with the National Board. Many US jurisdictions require it; see [National Board registration](/asme/national-board-registration).
- **R**: repairs and alterations to boilers and pressure vessels in service, under the NBIC.
- **VR**: repair of pressure relief valves.
- **NR**: repairs and replacements at nuclear facilities.
- **T/O**: testing of pressure relief valves.

## What the stamp means to a buyer

A stamp says the item was built under an accepted quality system and inspected by an [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector), and that a [data report](/asme/data-reports) exists for it. It says nothing about whether the design suits your process; that is set by the design conditions you specify. To get a stamp, see [how to get the U stamp](/asme/u-stamp).

title: US and Canadian boiler laws: who requires ASME
question: Is the ASME Code required by law in the US?
answer: The ASME Code isn't a federal law in the US. Most states, and every Canadian province, make it law by adopting it in their own boiler and pressure vessel acts, with their own inspection, registration and permit rules, and some don't regulate every kind of vessel. Check the jurisdiction where the equipment will be installed.
description: How US states and Canadian provinces make the ASME Code law: adoption, inspection, National Board registration, Canada's CRN.

sources.title: Boiler and Pressure Vessel Certificates of Authorization and the Certification Mark: Informational Handbook (BPV-GUI-03)
Registration

registration of data report forms may be required by the legal authority of a state or municipality of the United States or province of Canada.

body:
## How the Code becomes law

ASME is a standards body, not a regulator. The Code gets legal force when a **jurisdiction** (a state, a province, sometimes a city) adopts it in its boiler and pressure vessel law. The law then says which equipment is covered, which Code edition, who inspects it in service, and what has to be registered or permitted before it's operated.

What varies between jurisdictions:

- **Scope**: some regulate boilers and pressure vessels; some only boilers; many exempt small or low-pressure vessels.
- **Registration**: most US jurisdictions require the item's data report to be registered with the [National Board](/asme/national-board-registration) before installation.
- **Inspection in service**: by state inspectors or by insurance company inspectors holding National Board commissions, on set intervals.
- **Installation permits and operating certificates**.

## Who leads ASME reviews where

Jurisdictions also take part in certifying shops. ASME's handbook lists the states where the jurisdiction appoints the team leader for a [joint review](/asme/u-stamp) (Alaska, Delaware, Hawaii, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington), and says ASME appoints for Idaho, Wyoming, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands and all Canadian provinces, and the National Board for the remaining states.

## Canada

In Canada each province or territory regulates pressure equipment, generally by adopting CSA B51, which in turn uses the ASME Code. A design is registered with the province before construction and gets a **Canadian Registration Number (CRN)**, and fittings need one too. A vessel stamped to ASME but without a CRN can't be installed.

## How to check a jurisdiction

1. Find the state or provincial boiler and pressure vessel office for the installation site; the National Board keeps a listing of every jurisdiction's requirements and contacts.
2. Confirm: is this equipment in scope, which edition, is NB registration required, what inspection before first use.
3. Put the answers in the purchase order, so the [data report](/asme/data-reports) and nameplate come out right the first time.

This page doesn't list each state's rules: they change, and the jurisdiction's own office is the source. For buying from a shop outside the US, see [buying from India](/asme/buying-from-india).

title: How to get the ASME U stamp: steps, cost and timeline
question: How do you get an ASME U stamp?
answer: To get the U stamp a shop writes a quality control manual, signs an inspection agreement with an ASME-accredited Authorized Inspection Agency, applies to ASME through CA Connect with the fees, and passes a joint review: an on-site audit of the manual and a demonstration on real work or a mock-up. The certificate lasts three years.

they may be demonstrated using current work, a mock-up, or a combination of the two.
The written description and documentation which support understanding of the program must be in English.
