body:
## The steps

ASME's informational handbook sets out the route. In the order a shop usually does it:

1. **Decide the scope.** Which designator (U for Division 1 vessels), shop only or field work too, and any limits. The scope drives everything else; see [ASME stamps](/asme/stamps).
2. **Buy the Code books.** Current editions of every section the scope uses (ASME publishes the list per certificate). Copies aren't accepted.
3. **Write the quality control manual.** In English, covering every element the Code requires for the scope. See [the quality control manual](/asme/quality-control-manual).
4. **Sign an inspection agreement** with an ASME-accredited Authorized Inspection Agency. The agency's [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) will work with you on every stamped job.
5. **Apply** through ASME's CA Connect, with the deposit and fees, and return the signed ASME Accreditation/Certification Agreement.
6. **Prepare the demonstration.** Real Code work, a mock-up, or both, run through your system from drawing to data report: design calculations, material receipt and [MTRs](/asme/mtr), [WPS and PQR](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq), welder qualifications, NDE, a [hydrostatic test](/asme/hydrostatic-test) and a completed [data report](/asme/data-reports).
7. **The joint review.** A team leader (the ASME Designee) and a representative of your inspection agency audit the manual and watch the demonstration. They recommend issue to ASME, or list what must be fixed first.
8. **Certificate and stamp issued.** Valid for three years.

## Who leads the review

The ASME Designee is appointed by ASME, by the jurisdiction, or by the National Board, depending on where the shop is. The handbook names the US states where the jurisdiction appoints (Alaska, Delaware, Hawaii, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas, Washington), says ASME appoints for Idaho, Wyoming, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands and all Canadian provinces, and the National Board for the other states. See [US and Canadian boiler laws](/asme/state-boiler-laws).

## What it costs

ASME publishes its fees in its Price Guide; they change, so check the current one. The full cost to budget is more than ASME's fee:

- ASME's application and certificate fees, the review deposit, and the Designee's travel when ASME appoints;
- the inspection agency's fees for the review and then for every job it inspects;
- the Code books;
- staff time to write the manual and run the demonstration, and the demonstration item itself;
- any consultant who helps write the manual.

## How long it takes

There's no official timeline. The pace is usually set by the shop: writing a manual that matches how the shop really works, and getting a demonstration job through every step. Plan in months, not weeks, and book the review only when a full job can be shown end to end.

## Keeping it

The certificate lasts three years. Renewal is another joint review, and ASME must receive the renewal application at least six months before expiry. A shop with work in progress at expiry can ask for one six-month extension to finish that work.

## In India

The route is the same for a shop in India, and many Indian fabricators hold U and S certificates for export work. IBR 2026 lets an Indian Inspecting Authority inspect an export boiler to a foreign code; see [buying ASME equipment from India](/asme/buying-from-india) and [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: Welder continuity (QW-322): six-month rule and checker
question: How long is an ASME welder qualification valid?
answer: An ASME Section IX welder qualification has no fixed expiry date. Under QW-322 it lapses when the welder hasn't welded with that process for six months or more, and it can be revoked sooner if there's a reason to doubt their work. Each welding job resets the clock for that process, so a shop needs a record of every welder's last weld per process.
description: ASME welder continuity under QW-322: the six-month rule, renewing a lapsed qualification, the record to keep, and a free checker.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section IX: Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications)

body:
## The rule

Section IX's QW-322 sets two ways a welder's (or welding operator's) qualification ends:

1. **Six months without the process.** If the welder hasn't welded with a process for six months or more, their qualifications for that process lapse.
2. **Specific reason to question.** If there's a reason to doubt their ability to make welds that meet the specification, the qualifications supporting that work are revoked; the rest stay.

The clock is **per process**, not per WPS or per position. A welder qualified for SMAW and GTAW who only welds SMAW for seven months keeps SMAW and loses GTAW.

## What keeps it alive

Welding with the process, recorded. The record has to show the welder, the process and the date. Most shops log continuity from production weld maps or from a monthly sign-off sheet.

The checker above takes that log (welder, process, last weld date, one line each) and lists who lapses when, soonest first, with anyone within 30 days flagged. To keep the log itself, download the free [welder continuity log for Excel](/asme/welder-continuity-log.xlsx): one row per welder and process, with the lapse date, days left and status worked out for you, and lapsed or nearly lapsed rows coloured.

## Renewing a lapsed qualification

A lapsed qualification is renewed with a single test coupon in the process (QW-322.2), of any thickness, position and diameter, tested by bend tests or volumetric examination. Passing renews the welder's earlier qualifications for that process, with their original ranges. A revoked qualification is a different case: the welder retests for the work that was in question.

## The record an Inspector expects

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| Welder ID (their stamp) | Links to their WPQ and to welds on the weld map |
| Process | Continuity is per process |
| Date welded | Sets the next lapse date |
| Job or weld number | Evidence that it was real welding |
| Signed off by | Who confirmed it |

Keep it next to the WPQs; the [Authorized Inspector](/asme/authorized-inspector) checks continuity on every welder whose stamp appears on a job. A lapse found after welding means those welds were made by an unqualified welder. In a system that records who welded what and when, the lapse date is simply computed, which is what the checker does.

## Related

What the welder's test covers is in [welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification); how the WPQ relates to the WPS and PQR is in [WPS vs PQR vs WPQ](/asme/wps-pqr-wpq).

title: Welder qualification positions 1G to 6G explained
question: What does a 6G welding test qualify for?
answer: An ASME Section IX welder test qualifies a person for a process, a range of positions, thicknesses and pipe diameters, and a filler F-number. Positions go from 1G (flat) to 6G (pipe fixed at 45°). A 6G pipe test qualifies groove welds in all positions; plate tests qualify less on pipe. The test is checked by bend tests or by radiography.
description: ASME welder qualification (WPQ): 1G, 2G, 3G, 4G, 5G and 6G positions, what each qualifies, diameter and thickness limits, and bend vs radiography testing.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section IX: Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications)

body:
## The test positions

| Position | Plate | Pipe |
|---|---|---|
| 1G | Flat | Pipe horizontal, rolled while welding |
| 2G | Horizontal (vertical plate, horizontal weld) | Pipe vertical, weld runs horizontally around it |
| 3G | Vertical | (plate only) |
| 4G | Overhead | (plate only) |
| 5G | – | Pipe horizontal and fixed: the welder goes flat, vertical and overhead round it |
| 6G | – | Pipe fixed at 45°: every position in one weld |

F (1F to 5F) positions are the fillet weld equivalents.

## What a test qualifies

Section IX's position table (QW-461.9) sets what each test covers. The headline cases:

- **6G pipe**: groove welds in all positions, plate and pipe, and fillets in all positions.
- **2G plus 5G pipe** (two tests): the same as 6G.
- **3G and 4G plate**: plate in all positions, but pipe only above a large diameter, which is why pipe shops test on pipe.
- **1G**: flat only.

Diameter limits also apply (QW-452.3): a small-bore test coupon qualifies down to roughly its own size, and a coupon of 2⅞ in (73 mm) outside diameter or more qualifies that diameter and up. Thickness limits come from the deposited weld metal on the coupon.

## How the test is judged

- **Bend tests** (QW-302): coupons cut from the test weld and bent; cracks or openings beyond the limit fail.
- **Radiography or ultrasonic examination** (QW-302, QW-304): allowed instead of bends for most processes and materials, and much faster, but not for short-circuiting GMAW, which can hide lack of fusion.

## Welders and welding operators

A **welder** holds and guides the torch or electrode. A **welding operator** runs machine or automatic welding equipment, and has a separate, simpler qualification. The WPQ form records which.

## Keeping it

A welder's qualification doesn't expire on a calendar date: it lapses after six months without welding in the process. See [welder continuity](/asme/welder-continuity), and for the variables that force a retest, [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

In India, a boiler welder needs an IBR welder certificate as well; see [ASME vs IBR 2026](/asme/asme-vs-ibr).

title: WPS vs PQR vs WPQ: what each proves and how they link
question: What is the difference between a WPS and a PQR?
answer: A PQR records a test weld: the actual materials, settings and test results that prove a procedure makes sound welds. A WPS is the instruction a welder follows, written with ranges the PQR supports. A WPQ records that one welder passed their own test. In ASME Section IX the PQR comes first, the WPS cites it, and each welder needs a WPQ.
description: WPS, PQR and WPQ in ASME Section IX: what each document is, what goes in it, the tests behind it, and how a weld traces back through all three.

sources.title: 2025 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Section IX: Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications)

body:
## The three documents

| | PQR | WPS | WPQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full name | Procedure Qualification Record | Welding Procedure Specification | Welder (or Welding Operator) Performance Qualification |
| Proves | The procedure makes welds with the required strength and ductility | Nothing by itself; it's the instruction | This person can make a sound weld |
| Records | What was actually used on one test coupon, and the test results | Ranges for every variable, within what the PQR(s) support | The welder's test, results and what they're qualified for |
| Written | Once per test | From one or more PQRs | Once per welder per test |
| Signed by | The manufacturer, certifying the record is correct | The manufacturer | The manufacturer |

## The order a shop builds them

1. **Draft a WPS** for the job you want to weld (often called a pWPS until it's qualified).
2. **Weld a test coupon** to it and record every variable actually used.
3. **Test the coupon.** For a groove weld procedure, Section IX requires tension tests (for strength) and guided bend tests (for ductility): typically two tension and four bends, side bends for thicker coupons. Toughness tests are added when the construction code requires impact testing.
4. **Write the PQR** from the coupon record and the test results.
5. **Issue the WPS**, citing the PQR, with each variable's range set by what the PQR qualifies: thickness, materials, filler, position, preheat, heat treatment.
6. **Qualify each welder** on the WPS (or a test of their own), and record it on a WPQ.

Section IX doesn't allow a shop to use another company's PQR. The exception is AWS's Standard Welding Procedure Specifications, which Section IX accepts under conditions (in its QW-500 rules), with the shop demonstrating them first.

## Which changes need a new PQR

Every variable in Section IX is classified. Change an **essential** variable beyond what the PQR covers and you need a new PQR; change a **nonessential** one and you only revise the WPS. See [essential variables](/asme/essential-variables).

## Following one weld back

On a [data report](/asme/data-reports) package, any weld should trace like this: weld number on the weld map → welder's stamp → that welder's WPQ and [continuity](/asme/welder-continuity) → the WPS used → the PQR behind it → the filler metal's certificate and the base metal's [MTR](/asme/mtr). An Authorized Inspector will pick a weld and walk it. When those links live in different binders, this is where audits stall.

## Further reading

What a welder's test covers is in [welder qualification](/asme/welder-qualification); how materials are grouped so one test covers many is in [P-numbers](/asme/p-numbers); the whole of Section IX in outline is in [the Section IX guide](/asme/section-ix).

title: Custom vs off-the-shelf ERP for a small manufacturer
question: Should a small manufacturer build a custom ERP or buy one off the shelf?
answer: Buy off the shelf if your work fits a standard package, you can live with its scheduling and reports, and nobody in the business has time to own a software project. Build custom, in phases, when your workflow is what sets you apart, packages force workarounds that bring the spreadsheets back, and you can get in writing your data, the code and licence terms, and a fixed scope per phase. Many shops are best served in between.
description: Custom vs off-the-shelf ERP for small manufacturers: when each wins, the real costs over five years, one-builder risk, and questions to ask before you sign.

sources.title: ERP systems (forum discussion)
Free ERP system (forum discussion)

body:
## The short version

| Off-the-shelf wins when | Custom wins when |
|---|---|
| Your jobs move the way the package expects | The way you quote, schedule or trace is why customers pick you |
| You need to start in weeks, not months | Every package you've tried needs side spreadsheets to work |
| Nobody can spend time defining requirements | An owner or manager can spend a few hours a week shaping it |
| Per-user pricing stays small at your size | You'd pay for many modules and users to use a fraction |
| You want a large vendor's roadmap and user community | You want changes in days, decided by you |

Ahrom Labs builds custom systems, so read the rest knowing that. We've tried to make the case for buying as fairly as the case for building.

## What shop owners say

Owners debating this on Practical Machinist split along predictable lines:

- **For building:** custom software is cheaper to change than custom machinery; shops that built their own say they adjust it constantly and that order entry got much faster.
- **Against building:** large custom builds can cost far more and take far longer than planned; cheap builders sometimes don't finish; one shop that had a contractor build its system was glad of it but wouldn't advise writing your own.
- **Against buying big:** packages carry modules you never use, and the scheduling is often the weak part.
- **Middle paths:** low-code tools (Airtable, FileMaker), open-source ERPs (ERPNext, Odoo), or a configurable package with in-house customization.

## The costs to compare, over five years

Compare the same things on both sides, not a license price against a build quote:

| Cost | Off-the-shelf | Custom |
|---|---|---|
| Up front | Implementation, setup, data migration, training | The build, data migration, training |
| Every year | Subscription or maintenance per user, usually rising with headcount | Hosting, support and changes (a care plan) |
| Changes | Configuration if it allows it; otherwise workarounds | Paid changes, but anything is possible |
| Your time | Fitting your process to the package | Defining and testing what gets built |
| Leaving | Exporting data, usually in the vendor's format | Depends on the contract: get this in writing |

The hidden cost on the off-the-shelf side is the workaround: the spreadsheet that runs beside the ERP because it can't model one thing, and the person who keeps it. On the custom side it is dependence on one builder.

## Reducing the risk of custom

If you build, these protect you:

1. **Phases with a fixed scope and price each.** A prototype of one workflow on your own data first, then the build; never one large open-ended project.
2. **Your data, exportable any time,** in plain files, without asking.
3. **Code and licence terms in writing:** who owns the code, what licence you hold, and what happens to both if you stop paying for support.
4. **Documentation and a handover path,** so another developer could take over.
5. **Acceptance tests you write:** two or three of your real jobs, run end to end before go-live, like the [ten tests in our job shop ERP guide](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp).
6. **Keep the accounting system you trust.** A shop system that posts to QuickBooks is a smaller, safer project than one that replaces it ([QuickBooks beside a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)).

## Questions to ask a builder

- Show me a system you built that's been running for over a year, and let me talk to its owner.
- What happens on day one if you disappear? Where is the code and who can deploy it?
- How do changes get priced, and how fast do small ones happen?
- What's in the first phase, what isn't, and what's the price?
- How will my data come out if I leave?

The same comparison for Indian manufacturers, with TallyPrime and ERPNext in place of QuickBooks, is in [Tally vs ERPNext vs custom ERP](/notes/tally-vs-erpnext-vs-custom-erp). For the scheduling piece that packages most often get wrong, see [production scheduling software](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

title: ERP for job shops and small manufacturers: what to look for
question: What should a job shop look for in ERP software?
answer: A job shop ERP should carry each job from quote to invoice on one record: the quoted routing becomes the job, material is reserved for it, operations are scheduled on real machine capacity, the floor records time and scrap per operation, and actual cost is compared with the quote while the job is open. For a shop of 10 to 50 people, start with quoting, jobs, scheduling and job cost; keep QuickBooks for accounting; and test every vendor on two of your own jobs, not their sample data.
description: Job shop ERP explained for small manufacturers: the quote-to-invoice flow, what to buy first, testable requirements, and how to run a vendor demo on your jobs.

sources.title: Machine shop ERP recommendations (forum discussion)
ERP: JobBOSS2 vs ProShop vs something actually good (forum discussion)

body:
## One job, start to finish

A job shop makes to order, so the unit of work is the job, not the product. An ERP for one follows a job through every department on the same record:

1. **Quote**: material, operations, setup and run times, outside processing, price.
2. **Order**: the customer's PO turns the quote into a job with nothing typed again.
3. **Job and routing**: the quoted operations become the job's [routing](/systems/routing) and its traveler.
4. **Material**: stock is reserved for the job, or bought for it, with heat or lot numbers where they matter.
5. **Schedule**: operations placed on machines with real capacity ([how scheduling works](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software)).
6. **Shop floor**: operators record start, finish, quantity and scrap for each operation ([WIP tracking](/manufacturing/wip-tracking)).
7. **Quality**: inspection results and certificates attached to the job.
8. **Ship and invoice**: packing list, invoice from what shipped, posted to the accounting system.
9. **Job cost**: actual against quoted, per operation ([a worked example](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing)).

If two of these steps live in different files, that's where errors and lost hours collect.

## What to buy first

Not everything is equally urgent. For a shop of 10 to 50 people:

| First | Next | Usually later |
|---|---|---|
| Quoting from operations and times | Material reservation per job | Maintenance scheduling |
| Jobs and travelers from the quote | Purchasing from job shortages | Advanced planning (optimizers) |
| One shared schedule | Quality records and certificates | Customer portal |
| Shop-floor time per operation | Heat, lot or serial traceability | EDI with large customers |
| Job cost vs quote | Inventory by location | Multi-plant |

Accounting stays where it is. Most small manufacturers already run QuickBooks, and replacing it buys nothing; the ERP should post invoices and inventory value to it ([what QuickBooks covers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)).

## What shop owners warn about

Owners discussing ERP on forums such as Practical Machinist raise the same few points, and they are worth taking seriously:

- **Someone has to run it.** One experienced poster puts it plainly: a full ERP needs an administrator, which is real overhead for a 3 to 10 person shop.
- **Paying for what you don't use.** Large packages carry modules a small shop never touches, and the setup effort that comes with them.
- **Weak scheduling.** Several owners say the scheduling module was the weak part: not good enough to plan the floor day to day.
- **The workflow bends to the software.** If the system can't model how your jobs move, people keep the old spreadsheets, and now there are two sources of truth.

## Ten requirements you can test in a demo

Each of these can be checked in an hour with your own data. A vendor that can't show one live is telling you something.

1. Turn one of your recent quotes into a job without retyping the operations.
2. Show the job's traveler with each operation, machine and quoted time.
3. Reserve stock for the job, then show that a second job can't plan on the same material.
4. Schedule five jobs on your machines and shifts, then add a rush order and show what moves.
5. Record an operation's time and scrap from a phone or a shop-floor screen.
6. Show estimated vs actual cost for a job before it ships.
7. Find which jobs used a given heat or lot number, and the reverse.
8. Ship part of a job and invoice only what shipped.
9. Post that invoice to QuickBooks once, retry the post, and show there's still one invoice.
10. Export every record (jobs, routings, stock, costs) to files you can open without the vendor.

The last one matters more than it looks: it's what makes leaving possible. If a vendor leads with AI, add the tests in [AI in ERP: what it can safely do today](/ai-assistant/ai-in-erp).

## Packaged, configurable or built for you

Three routes, each right for some shops (compared in more depth in [custom vs off-the-shelf ERP](/manufacturing/custom-vs-off-the-shelf-erp)):

- **Packaged job shop ERP.** Fastest to start if your work fits its model. You adapt to the software, pay per user, and live with its scheduling and reports.
- **Configurable platform.** A general ERP or low-code base set up for you. More flexible, but someone keeps the configuration working.
- **Built for your workflow.** Fits exactly and can change as you do. It costs more up front and depends on the builder staying around, so get in writing that you can export all your data at any time, what happens to the code and the licence if you stop paying for support, and a fixed scope per phase.

Ahrom Labs builds the third kind: operations systems for manufacturers and distributors, in phases, beside the accounting software you already use. Two things we've built show what "fits the workflow" means in practice: a cutting record where every plate cut puts its usable remnant back into stock, with weights that always add up ([remnants back into stock](/notes/plate-remnants-back-into-stock)), and a customer portal that shows each order's stage from the records departments already keep ([one order, every department](/notes/customer-portal-one-order-every-department)). Both run at a manufacturer in India; our US offer starts with a fixed-price prototype of one workflow, shown below.

Whatever you choose, take two of your own jobs to every demo, the [QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory) questions if stock is your pain, and the ten tests above.

title: Free job shop production schedule template (Excel)
question: Is there a free production scheduling template in Excel for a job shop?
answer: Yes. This free Excel template plans a job shop by machine: list each job's operations in routing order with their hours and a planned day, and it flags any operation planned after the job's due date or before its previous operation, and shows the hours booked on each machine each day in red when they exceed that machine's shift. It suits up to a few dozen open jobs and one planner; past that, use scheduling software.
description: A free Excel production schedule template for job shops: routings by machine, planned days, due-date checks and daily machine load against shift hours.
body:
## Download

[**Job shop schedule template (Excel)**](/manufacturing/job-shop-schedule-template.xlsx), free under CC BY 4.0. It opens in Excel or Google Sheets and needs no macros.

It is filled in with the six made-up jobs from the [schedule demo](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software), so you can see it working before you replace them with your own.

## What's in it

| Sheet | What you enter | What it works out |
|---|---|---|
| **Machines** | Each machine or work center and its hours per day (8 for one shift, 16 for two) | Nothing; the other sheets read it |
| **Jobs** | One row per operation, in routing order: job, due date, operation number, machine, hours, planned day | A check on every row: OK, "After due date", or "Before previous operation" |
| **Load** | The first day of the plan | Hours booked per machine for each of the next 20 working days, red where a machine is over its hours |

The machine column is a drop-down from the Machines sheet, so a typo can't create a machine that doesn't exist.

## How to use it

1. List your machines and their shift hours.
2. Enter each open job's operations from its [routing](/systems/routing), with the quoted hours. If your quotes are built from operations and times, copy them; that's also what [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) compares against.
3. Give each operation a planned day, earliest due date first, and each operation no earlier than the one before it.
4. Look at the Load sheet. Red means that machine has more hours booked than it has that day: move an operation, split it across days, or add a shift.
5. Fix every "After due date" either by moving work or by telling the customer now, not on the due date.

The sample shows the point of step 4. Three days come up red, and the welding cell on Wednesday is the real problem: 13 hours booked on an 8-hour day, which is why frame job J-103 runs late in the demo. The other two (the laser on Monday, the press brake on Tuesday, 9 hours each) are operations that run over into the next day, which the template counts on the day they start.

## Its limits

A spreadsheet schedule is honest about what it is:

- **One planner.** Two people editing copies of it will drift apart; owners on forums say this is where spreadsheets break.
- **Nothing moves by itself.** When an operation slips, you move the later ones by hand. Scheduling software moves the whole chain ([finite capacity](/systems#finite-capacity-scheduling)).
- **It doesn't know what's finished.** Progress has to be typed in; without it the plan drifts from the floor. That's what [WIP tracking](/manufacturing/wip-tracking) fixes.
- **Hours land on one day.** An operation's hours all count on its planned day, so long operations show as an overload; split them into one row per day if that matters.

When those limits cost you late jobs every week, read [what production scheduling software does](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software) and try the demo with your own jobs.

title: Production scheduling software for job shops: machines, shifts and due dates
question: What does production scheduling software do in a job shop?
answer: Production scheduling software places each job's operations on the machines that can run them, in routing order, within the hours each machine is staffed, and shows which jobs will miss their due date before it happens. In a job shop it replaces the spreadsheet or whiteboard with one shared schedule, built from each job's routing, real shift hours and due dates, that updates when a rush order arrives or a machine goes down.
description: How production scheduling software works in a job shop: finite capacity, routings, shifts, due dates, dispatch rules vs optimizers, and a live demo.

sources.title: Machine scheduling (forum discussion)
Machine scheduling software, not quite ERP (forum discussion)

body:
## What a schedule needs to know

A schedule is only as good as four inputs. Most bad schedules are missing one of them:

| Input | What it is | Where it usually lives today |
|---|---|---|
| **Routing** for each job | The operations in order, the machine or work center for each, setup and run time | In the estimator's head, or on the quote |
| **Capacity** | Which machines exist, their shifts, planned downtime | On the wall, or nowhere |
| **Due dates** | When each job must ship | In the order, or the customer's email |
| **Material** | Whether the material for each job is in stock or due in | In QuickBooks or the stores, often out of date |

A [routing](/systems/routing) is the piece shops most often lack. If quotes are built from operations and times, the routing already exists; see [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing), where the same times become the estimate.

## Finite and infinite capacity

**Infinite capacity** scheduling works backward from the due date and assumes every machine is free when needed. It answers "when must this start?" and is how classic MRP plans. It is why a schedule can show the laser booked for 30 hours on a Tuesday.

**[Finite capacity](/systems#finite-capacity-scheduling)** scheduling only books a machine for the hours it has. When the laser is full, the next job waits, and its later operations move with it. That answers the question customers actually ask: "when will it ship?"

The demo above is finite. With one shift, the five sample jobs all ship on time. Add a rush order due tomorrow and it goes first, and frame job J-103 slips a day, because both the rush job and J-103 need the welding cell and the weld cell is the bottleneck. Switch to two shifts and everything ships on time again. That is the trade a scheduler weighs every day, made visible.

## How the software decides the order

Three approaches, from simplest to most complex:

1. **Dispatch rules.** Take jobs in a fixed order (earliest due date first is the common one, as in the demo) and give each operation the first slot its machine and the previous operation allow. Predictable: a planner can check any result by hand.
2. **Optimizers (APS).** Advanced planning and scheduling tools search many orders to cut lateness or changeovers. Better on paper, but harder to explain, and a plan nobody understands tends to be overridden on the floor.
3. **People with a tool.** The planner drags jobs around a board; the software checks capacity and shows the knock-on effect. Most small shops land here.

For a shop of 10 to 50 people, a dispatch rule plus a planner who can override it usually beats an optimizer. The bigger win is having one schedule everyone trusts.

## Where AI fits, and where it doesn't

AI is useful around the schedule: reading a new order's drawing or email into a draft routing, warning that a job is drifting late, or explaining in plain words why J-103 moved. It shouldn't decide machine assignments by itself. A schedule must respect hard limits, such as machine hours, routing order and material on hand, and a rule or solver can guarantee those; a language model can't. Our rule: AI drafts and explains, rules and people decide, the same split we use where a suggestion ends up on a quality document ([same confidence, different autonomy](/notes/same-confidence-different-autonomy)). More on what AI can safely do across an ERP: [AI in ERP](/ai-assistant/ai-in-erp).

## Why the spreadsheet stops working

Shop owners on Practical Machinist describe the same path: a sheet with one column per machine and a row per day, or a whiteboard, which works while one person owns it. It breaks when:

- two or three people edit it, and the copies drift apart;
- a job's later operations don't move when its first one slips;
- nobody can say when a new order could ship without redoing the whole sheet;
- the floor's actual progress never makes it back, so the plan slowly turns into fiction.

The last point is the real limit. A schedule needs to know what has actually finished, which means operators recording each operation as they complete it, the same data [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) needs; see [WIP tracking with barcoded travelers](/manufacturing/wip-tracking).

If you're not ready for software, the free [job shop schedule template](/manufacturing/production-schedule-template) does the capacity check in Excel.

## What to ask a vendor

- Does it schedule to finite capacity, per machine and shift, or only backward from due dates?
- Can it take the routing straight from the quote?
- What happens to a job's later operations when an earlier one runs late?
- Can a planner override a slot without breaking the rest?
- How does finished work get back from the floor, and how quickly?
- Does it check material before scheduling a job?

Bring two or three of your own jobs to the demo and ask them to schedule them live. For choosing the rest of the system, see [ERP for job shops](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp); for where scheduling sits next to QuickBooks, see [does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing).

title: Does QuickBooks work for manufacturing? Edition by edition
question: Does QuickBooks work for manufacturing?
answer: Partly, and it depends on the edition. QuickBooks Online Plus and Advanced track inventory and job costs but have no bills of materials or manufacturing orders; Intuit says its manufacturing features are only in Intuit Enterprise Suite, which still doesn't support multi-level bills of materials. QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise (Manufacturing & Wholesale) goes furthest. None of them, by Intuit's own pages, schedules machines or tracks time by operation, so most job shops keep QuickBooks for the books and run the shop in a separate system.

body:
## The short answer, by edition

Checked against Intuit's own pages on 2 November 2026. Intuit changes plans often; check yours before relying on this.

| | QuickBooks Online Plus / Advanced | Intuit Enterprise Suite | QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise (Manufacturing & Wholesale) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory quantities and value | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Bill of materials and assemblies | No | Yes, single level only | Yes, including subassemblies |
| Manufacturing (build) orders | No | Yes: planned, in progress, completed | Yes: build orders |
| Component shortages | No | Yes, a shortage report | Yes: how many you can build from stock |
| Labor in product cost | Through projects, not per unit | As a service line on the bill of materials | Yes |
| Multiple warehouses, bins, lots, serials | Not described in Intuit's inventory setup article | Not described in Intuit's manufacturing help | Advanced Inventory, Platinum and Diamond only |
| Routings, machines, operations | No | Not described in Intuit's help | Not described on Intuit's product page |
| Machine scheduling, shop-floor time by operation | No | Not described | Not described (production forecasts and labor planning are) |

"Not described" means the Intuit page we checked doesn't mention it; ask Intuit or a ProAdvisor if it matters to you.

## Three different things called "manufacturing"

Most confusion comes from mixing up three things a shop needs:

1. **What a part is made of**: the [bill of materials](/systems#bill-of-materials). QuickBooks' assembly items cover this, in the editions that have them.
2. **How it is made**: the [routing](/systems/routing), the operations in order (cut, bend, weld, inspect), on which machine, with setup and run times. No QuickBooks edition models this.
3. **When it is made**: the schedule, which puts each operation on a machine with real capacity. See [production scheduling software](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

A shop that buys and assembles kits mostly needs the first. A job shop that machines, cuts or welds to order needs all three, which is why job shops outgrow QuickBooks sooner than assemblers do.

## QuickBooks Online Plus and Advanced

Inventory is included in Plus and Advanced: quantity on hand, reorder points, purchase orders, and either FIFO or moving average cost, chosen once (see [QuickBooks Online inventory for manufacturers](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory)). What's missing for a manufacturer:

- **No bills of materials or builds.** Intuit's manufacturing help says these features are in Intuit Enterprise Suite; if you downgrade from it, bills of materials become view-only.
- **Bundles are not assemblies.** A bundle groups items so they go on an invoice together; no finished part sits in stock and no labor goes into its cost.
- **Job costing is by project.** Plus and Advanced group a customer's income, expenses and timesheets into a project. That gives job profit, but not setup and run hours per operation (see [job costing in QuickBooks](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing)).

A common workaround is to keep raw material as non-inventory items and adjust finished goods by hand. It keeps the books roughly right but hides what each job really used.

## Intuit Enterprise Suite

Intuit Enterprise Suite is Intuit's cloud plan above QuickBooks Online Advanced. Its manufacturing feature works like this:

- An **inventory assembly item** carries a bill of materials: components, raw materials and services such as labor for one unit. A manufacturing order can't start without one.
- A **manufacturing order** starts as Planned and reserves its components; a shortage column counts what other open orders need from the same stock.
- Completing the order creates a **build assembly** that moves components into finished stock and computes the actual cost. Estimated cost comes from each component's default purchase cost.

The limits that matter to a job shop: bills of materials are single level (no subassemblies), edits to a bill apply only to new orders, and Intuit's help doesn't describe routings, work centers or scheduling. It suits a shop that assembles from bought parts more than one that machines from bar stock.

## QuickBooks Desktop Enterprise, Manufacturing & Wholesale

Desktop Enterprise has the deepest manufacturing features of the three: bills of materials with subassemblies, automated builds and purchase orders for the components a final assembly needs, and costs from raw material to finished goods including labor and landed cost. Its **Advanced Inventory** (multiple locations down to bin, lot and serial numbers, barcode scanning, cycle counts) is in the Platinum and Diamond subscriptions only; landed cost and sales order fulfillment are too.

It is Windows software (hosted versions exist), sold by subscription, and Intuit's page doesn't describe routing by machine or shop-floor time by operation.

## Signs the shop has outgrown QuickBooks

From what shop owners describe on forums such as Practical Machinist, and what we see in our own work:

- Quotes live in a spreadsheet and the job is set up again from scratch when the order arrives.
- The schedule is a whiteboard or a sheet with one column per machine, and only one person trusts it.
- You find out a job lost money weeks after it shipped, when the bills arrive.
- Stock in QuickBooks and stock on the shelf disagree, because material used on the floor is entered later, or never.
- Two people keep "the real list" of open jobs, and they differ.

None of these is a QuickBooks bug. QuickBooks is an accounting system; these are operations problems.

## Keep QuickBooks, add a shop system

For most small manufacturers the cheapest sound setup is QuickBooks for the books and a shop system for the work, with one owner for each record:

| Record | Owned by | Goes to the other system as |
|---|---|---|
| Customers and vendors | Either, but only one | A copy, kept in step |
| Quotes, jobs, routings, schedule | Shop system | Nothing (stays in operations) |
| Shop-floor hours, scrap, material used | Shop system | Job cost, and the inventory value at month-end |
| Customer invoices | Shop system (from the shipped job) | An invoice, posted once |
| Vendor bills and payments | QuickBooks | Status read back to the shop system |
| Chart of accounts, tax, payroll | QuickBooks | Nothing |

"Owned by" means people change that record in one place only. Everything that breaks between two systems starts with a record two people can edit in both.

## Connecting the two without duplicates

Our QuickBooks Online connector is being built; it isn't live yet. The rules it follows are the ones our [TallyPrime connection](/notes/connecting-tallyprime-four-ways) already runs on:

- **Post once, by our own number.** Each invoice carries the shop system's document number; before posting, the connector checks whether that number already exists, so a retry can't create a second copy.
- **Read back, don't assume.** After posting, read the record from the accounting system and store its ID and totals ([reconcile against the source of truth](/patterns/reconcile-against-source-of-truth)).
- **Fail loudly.** A rejected entry (a missing account, a closed period) waits for a person with the reason shown, instead of retrying forever or being dropped ([failures flagged, not lost](/patterns/failures-flagged-not-lost)).
- **Nobody re-keys.** On Intuit's community, many "duplicate" problems come from someone entering by hand what an integration had already posted, which also takes the stock out twice.

## Is QuickBooks an ERP?

No. An ERP covers operations (orders, production, stock, purchasing) as well as accounting, on one database. QuickBooks is accounting software with some inventory; Intuit Enterprise Suite and Desktop Enterprise add manufacturing pieces but not shop-floor control. That's fine: many good shop systems are built to sit beside QuickBooks rather than replace it. See [ERP for job shops](/manufacturing/job-shop-erp) for what the shop side needs.

title: Job costing in QuickBooks for manufacturers: estimated vs actual
question: Can QuickBooks do job costing for a manufacturer?
answer: QuickBooks Online Plus, Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite do job costing through projects: each customer job collects its invoices, bills, expenses and timesheets, and shows profit. That works for a contractor. A machine shop also needs setup and run hours, machine time, scrap and rework per job, compared with what was quoted while the job is still open. QuickBooks doesn't split cost that way, so shops either keep a job-cost sheet beside it or track it in a shop system.

body:
## What QuickBooks job costing does

In QuickBooks Online Plus, Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite, a **project** groups one customer job's invoices, estimates, bills, expenses and timesheets, with an income, cost and profit view. Intuit's own example is an auto repair job that tracks every part and labor hour.

Labor reaches a project two ways, per Intuit's help:

- **Payroll expenses**: real wages, taxes and workers' comp, posted after each payroll run.
- **Estimated hourly costs**: hours on project timesheets times a fixed rate per employee, which can include overhead. Visible straight away, but only for time tracked after the rate was set.

The project profitability report uses payroll expenses only. Intuit Enterprise Suite, and Advanced with the construction add-on, also offer basic or detailed project costing; once you pick detailed you can't switch back.

## What a manufacturer needs that projects don't split

A project answers "did this job make money?" after the costs arrive. A shop needs to know why, while it can still act:

| Cost a shop tracks | In a QuickBooks project |
|---|---|
| Material issued to the job | Only if bought for that job, or adjusted by hand |
| Setup hours vs run hours | One timesheet total per person |
| Machine time (the shop rate) separate from labor | No: an hourly rate per employee, not per machine |
| Scrapped parts and rework | Not separated from normal production |
| Outside processing (plating, heat treat) | Yes, as bills assigned to the project |
| Quoted hours per operation, to compare | No |

Machine time matters most. In a machine shop the machine and its overhead often cost more per hour than the operator, and one operator may run two machines. A rate per employee can't show that.

## A worked example

Every figure here is made up. A shop quotes 200 steel brackets at $18.50 each. Labor costs $32 an hour; the shop rate (machine plus overhead) is $65 per machine hour, so an hour of setup or run time costs $97.

| | Estimated | Actual |
|---|---:|---:|
| Material | $840.00 (200 × $4.20) | $910.00 (200 × $4.55) |
| Setup | $194.00 (2 h) | $339.50 (3.5 h) |
| Run time | $1,940.00 (6 min each) | $2,425.00 (7.5 min each) |
| Outside processing | $300.00 | $300.00 |
| Scrapped parts (8 made again) | $0.00 | $133.40 |
| Rework | $0.00 | $145.50 (1.5 h) |
| **Total cost** | **$3,274.00** | **$4,253.40** |
| Revenue | $3,700.00 | $3,700.00 |
| **Margin** | **$426.00 (11.5%)** | **−$553.40 (−15.0%)** |

The job was quoted at 22 hours and took 31: **1.41 hours used per hour quoted**. The largest part of the $979.40 miss is run time ($485.00, from a cycle 25% slower than quoted), not the scrap that people notice on the floor. The calculator above has the same job; change any figure.

One owner on Practical Machinist describes the habit that fixes quoting: log estimated and actual time side by side on every job, and when a few months of similar jobs show the same miss, raise the quoted time by that much. The hours factor is that number.

## Doing it with QuickBooks and a spreadsheet

1. Turn on projects and create one per job.
2. Assign material bills and outside processing to the project as they arrive.
3. Have operators record time per job daily, before they clock out; split setup from run if you can ([how shops get operators to scan](/manufacturing/wip-tracking)).
4. Keep the quoted hours and material per job in a sheet beside it. The free [job cost workbook](/manufacturing/job-cost-worked-example.xlsx) has the columns and formulas, with this example filled in.
5. Close each job by comparing the two, and feed the hours factor back into the next quote.

It works for a handful of jobs a week. It strains when material is issued from stock rather than bought per job, when one operator runs two machines, or when you want the answer before the job ships.

## When to move job costing into a shop system

Move it when the comparison arrives too late to matter. A shop system records material issued, setup and run time and scrap against each operation as they happen, compares them with the quoted routing while the job is open, and posts only the invoice and the inventory value to QuickBooks (see [keeping QuickBooks beside a shop system](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing)). Material reserved per job keeps the material line honest; see [QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory). And costing depends on where the hours were planned: [production scheduling](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software).

title: QuickBooks Online inventory: what it tracks and where manufacturers outgrow it
question: Is QuickBooks Online inventory management enough for a manufacturer?
answer: QuickBooks Online Plus and Advanced track how many of each item you have, what it's worth (FIFO or moving average cost, chosen once), what's on order and when to reorder. That covers a reseller. A manufacturer usually also needs raw material, work in progress and finished parts kept apart, material set aside for each job, and stock by location or lot, which QuickBooks Online's inventory doesn't describe. That is the point to add a stock layer beside it.
description: QuickBooks Online inventory for manufacturers: plans, FIFO or average cost, reorder points, and the gaps: WIP, job reservations, locations, lots and BOMs.

body:
## What QuickBooks Online inventory does

From Intuit's help pages, checked on 2 November 2026:

| Feature | QuickBooks Online |
|---|---|
| Plans | Plus and Advanced; Simple Start and Essentials can buy an inventory add-on or upgrade |
| Quantity on hand | Goes down with each invoice or sales receipt, up with each receipt from a vendor |
| Reordering | Reorder points and low-stock alerts; purchase orders and what's still on order |
| Valuation | FIFO or moving average cost (MAC), chosen once: it can't be changed later, and an item created before choosing defaults to FIFO |
| Item types | Inventory, non-inventory (tracked as cost, not quantity), service, and bundles that group items on a sales form |
| Reports | Stock on hand, best sellers, cost of goods sold |

For a business that buys finished products and sells them, that is a complete inventory system.

## Where a manufacturer runs out of room

A manufacturer's stock moves through stages QuickBooks Online doesn't model:

- **No raw, in-progress and finished stages.** Material issued to a job isn't stock on the shelf any more, but it isn't a finished part yet either. QuickBooks Online has no [work in progress](/systems/work-in-progress); material sits in stock until someone adjusts it.
- **No bills of materials or builds.** Turning components into a finished part is an Intuit Enterprise Suite feature, not a QuickBooks Online one. See [does QuickBooks work for manufacturing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-for-manufacturing).
- **No material set aside per job.** Quantity on hand tells you what's on the shelf, not what is already promised. Without a [stock reservation](/systems/stock-reservation), two jobs can plan on the same bar stock and the second finds out on the floor.
- **One pool of stock.** Intuit's inventory setup article doesn't describe warehouses, bins, lots or serial numbers. On Intuit's community the usual workarounds are a separate item per location or location codes in item names, which multiplies the item list.
- **Counts arrive late.** Stock changes when someone enters a transaction. Material taken on the floor and entered at week's end means the number is wrong all week.

## What changes when you add a stock layer

The usual fix is not to leave QuickBooks but to keep stock movements in an operations system and send QuickBooks the accounting result:

| In the stock layer | In QuickBooks |
|---|---|
| Every receipt, issue to a job, return, transfer and count, scanned as it happens | Purchase bills and the inventory asset value |
| Raw, in-progress and finished quantities per item and location | Cost of goods sold when invoiced |
| Material reserved against each job, oldest stock first | Nothing: reservations aren't accounting |
| Lots, heat numbers or serials, and which job used them | Nothing |

The [QR inventory and order reservations](/services/inventory-and-reservations) system we built for an electronic components trader works this way: whole reels reserved per customer order line, two stores, scanning in and out, with a manager's override needed to ship reserved stock elsewhere ([how the reels and boxes work](/notes/reels-boxes-and-two-stores)). The US build of that system is open as a live demo with sample logins.

## When to stay, when to move

Stay on QuickBooks Online inventory if you resell more than you make, have one location, and can count everything in an afternoon. Add a stock layer when material is issued to jobs, when two jobs compete for the same stock, when you need lot or heat traceability, or when the shelf and the books disagree every month. For costing those jobs, see [job costing in QuickBooks](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing).

title: WIP tracking with barcoded job travelers
question: How do you track work in progress on a shop floor?
answer: Give every job a traveler with a barcode, list its operations in order, and have operators scan the job at each operation's start and finish, with the good and scrapped quantities. That one habit shows where every job is, what's queued in front of each machine, the actual hours for job costing, and the value of work in progress for the books. Fixed scan stations work better than tablets on most shop floors.
description: How to track work in progress (WIP) in a job shop: travelers, scan points, a work order example, stations vs tablets, getting operators to scan.

sources.title: Paperless (or less paper) job tracking and routing, job shop specific (forum discussion)
Computers and tablets on the shop floor (forum discussion)

body:
## What WIP tracking records

[Work in progress](/systems/work-in-progress) is every job that has started and not shipped. Tracking it means recording a small set of events, always against a job and an operation:

| Event | Who records it | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| Material issued to the job | Stores | Stock leaves the shelf and becomes WIP cost |
| Operation started | Operator | Where the job is; queue time before it |
| Operation finished, with good and scrapped quantity | Operator | Actual run time and scrap per operation |
| Inspection passed or held | Quality | Whether it can move on |
| Job finished and packed | Shipping | WIP becomes finished goods, ready to invoice |

Each scan moves the job from one state to the next ([state transitions](/systems#state-transition)), so the system can refuse impossible moves, such as finishing an operation that never started or shipping a job still waiting for inspection.

## A work order example

The [job traveler](/systems#job-traveler) is the work order as it travels with the parts. A made-up example for 200 steel brackets:

| Op | Operation | Machine | Setup (h) | Run (min each) | Started | Finished | Good | Scrap |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| 10 | Laser cut blanks | Laser | 0.5 | 1.0 | Tue 07:10 | Tue 11:05 | 208 | 0 |
| 20 | Bend, two flanges | Press brake | 1.0 | 1.5 | Tue 12:30 | Wed 09:40 | 200 | 8 |
| 30 | Weld gusset | Weld cell | 0.5 | 3.0 | Wed 10:15 | | | |
| 40 | Inspect, first and last piece | Quality | | | | | | |
| 50 | Powder coat | Outside vendor | | | | | | |

The header carries the job number (and its barcode), customer, part number and revision, quantity, due date, material with heat or lot number, and the drawing. Times and quantities come from scans, not handwriting. The quoted setup and run times on each line are what [job costing](/manufacturing/quickbooks-job-costing) compares the actual times against.

## Scan stations or tablets

Owners discussing this on Practical Machinist land in roughly the same place:

- **Fixed stations** (a screen and scanner at each work center, or one per area) survive coolant and dust, don't get dropped or walk off, and stay on a wired network.
- **Tablets** are convenient and have a camera that reads barcodes, but touchscreens get dirty, they're dropped or misplaced, and slow Wi-Fi in a metal building makes every scan a wait.
- **Phones** work for stores and shipping, where people move around anyway.

A common setup: a barcode on the paper traveler, a cheap scanner at each station, phones for stores.

## Getting operators to scan

Software is the easy part. What makes it stick, from shops that have done it:

- **One scan, not a form.** Scan the job, scan your badge, type a quantity. Anything longer gets skipped.
- **Tie it to pay.** When the same scans fill timesheets, people scan, because it pays them.
- **Say what it's for.** Scanning can feel like surveillance; it lands better framed as "so nobody has to walk the floor to find a job".
- **Watch for gaming**, such as closing an operation early. Compare scans with the schedule and look at outliers, not everyone.
- **Do it daily.** Time recorded at the end of the day, before clocking out, is close enough; time recorded at the end of the week is fiction.

## When it pays off

One owner on Practical Machinist puts the break-even around seven to ten people. Below that, the owner can see every job from the office door, and manual counts in QuickBooks may be enough. Above it, nobody can, and WIP tracking is what makes a [schedule](/manufacturing/production-scheduling-software) trustworthy: the plan knows what has actually finished. The accounting side matters too: WIP is an asset on the balance sheet, which QuickBooks Online doesn't hold as a stage of its own ([QuickBooks Online inventory](/manufacturing/quickbooks-online-inventory)).
